title: How we see: light goes straight, a lens makes a sharp picture, and two eyes build depth

summary.text: Hold a finger up at arm's length and close one eye, then the other. The finger jumps sideways against the wall, though it never moved. Your child tests whether light can ever go round a corner, makes a lens form an upside-down picture of a window, and measures how far a pencil seems to jump when it is near and when it is far. The jump is how the brain works out distance. Nobody yet knows how two flat pictures from two eyes become one solid world.
summary.art: A child at a table holding one finger up in front of a plain wall, with two dotted copies of the finger showing where it seems to be with the left eye and the right eye.

intro.hook: Hold one finger up at arm's length, in front of a plain wall. Close your left eye and look at the finger. Now open the left eye and close the right. What happened to your finger? Did the finger move, or did something else?
intro.text: The finger did not move. But each of your eyes looks from a slightly different place, so each gets a slightly different picture. Your brain joins the two into one, and it uses the difference to tell how far away things are. In this unit you find out how light travels from the world to your eyes in straight lines. You build a lens that makes a picture of a window. Then you measure the jump, and find out how much of what you see is worked out and not simply seen.
intro.art: Two panels of the same child's view, one with the left eye closed and one with the right eye closed, with a finger in different places against a wall.

outcomes: I can show with a test that light travels in straight lines, and say what happens when something is in the way.
I can draw a ray diagram, with arrows, to show how light from a lamp reaches my eye.
I can explain why an eye needs a lens, and why the picture on the retina is upside down.
I can explain how the lens changes shape to focus on near and far things.
I can explain why two eyes give us depth, using what I measured in the finger jump test.
I can say where the eyes of hunting and hunted animals sit, and what each gains.
I can fill in a results table, compare it with my guess, and finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.
I can say what scientists agree about seeing, and what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: A straight line with an arrow that shows the path of a thin beam of light.
terms.example: A torch beam through a hole in a card follows one straight ray.
terms.art: A torch shining through a hole in a card with a straight arrow drawn along the beam.

terms.meaning: A drawing that uses straight arrows to show how light travels from a source, to a thing, to an eye.
terms.example: A drawing of a lamp, a mango and an eye with arrows from the lamp to the mango and from the mango to the eye.
terms.art: A lamp, a mango and an eye with straight arrows between them.

terms.meaning: A clear, curved piece of glass, plastic or jelly that bends light so that it comes together. It is thicker in the middle than at the edges.
terms.example: A magnifying glass is a lens. The clear lens inside your eye is a lens too.
terms.art: A magnifying glass and a drawing of the lens inside an eye, side by side.

terms.meaning: To bring the rays from one point of a thing together at one point, so that the picture is sharp, not blurry.
terms.example: A camera focuses on a face, so the face is sharp and the wall behind is blurry.
terms.art: A sharp picture of a face next to a blurry picture of the same face.

terms.meaning: The thin layer at the back of the eye that catches the light. A sharp picture forms on it.
terms.example: A picture of a window forms upside down on your retina when you look at a window.
terms.art: A cutaway eye with a small upside-down window picture on the retina.

terms.meaning: A tiny pit in the middle of the retina packed with cone cells. It is the part of your eye that sees finest detail.
terms.example: When you read a word, you point your fovea at each letter in turn.
terms.art: A retina with a small yellow spot in the middle labelled fovea.

terms.meaning: Using two eyes together. The two eyes see the same scene from two slightly different places.
terms.example: Two eyes are what let you catch a ball thrown to you.
terms.art: A child looking at a ball with two eyes, and two slightly different views drawn in thought bubbles.

terms.meaning: The way a near thing seems to move sideways more than a far thing when you change where you look from.
terms.example: When you look out of a bus window, a nearby tree zips past while a far hill hardly moves.
terms.art: A bus window with a close tree and a distant hill, and arrows showing the tree moving more.

terms.meaning: How far away different things are from you. A picture on a flat page has no real depth, but it can show clues to it.
terms.example: In a room, the table is nearer than the window, and the window is nearer than the tree outside.
terms.art: A room seen from above with the distances to a table, a window and a tree marked.

terms.meaning: How much of the world you can see at once without moving your eyes or head.
terms.example: A horse can see almost all the way round without turning their head.
terms.art: A top-down drawing of a person and a horse, each with a wedge showing the field of view.

terms.meaning: What you see at the edges of your field of view. It is good at noticing movement, but poor at fine detail and colour.
terms.example: You notice a bus coming from the side before you can say its colour.
terms.art: A child looking straight ahead while a dim moving shape comes in from the side.

terms.meaning: A condition where near things are sharp but far things are blurry, because the eye focuses in front of the retina. Glasses with a curved-in lens fix it.
terms.example: A short-sighted child can read a book easily but cannot read the blackboard.
terms.art: An eye with rays meeting in front of the retina, and a glasses lens that moves them back.

terms.meaning: A condition where far things are easier than near things, because the eye focuses behind the retina. Glasses with a curved-out lens fix it.
terms.example: Many older people hold a newspaper at arm's length, to make the letters sharp.
terms.art: An eye with rays meeting behind the retina, and a reading lens that moves them forward.

terms.meaning: The closest distance at which your eye can still make a sharp picture of a thing.
terms.example: Bring a pencil tip slowly towards your nose. The place where it turns blurry is your near point.
terms.art: A child bringing a pencil toward her nose, with a ruler showing the distance where it blurs.

terms.meaning: How wide a thing looks to your eye. It depends on both the size of the thing and its distance from you.
terms.example: A person standing 8 metres away looks half as tall as the same person 4 metres away.
terms.art: Two people at different distances with lines from their heads and feet meeting at an eye, making a narrow and a wide angle.

terms.meaning: A picture or scene that your brain reads wrongly, even when you know the facts.
terms.example: Two lines of the same length can look different if they have different ends.
terms.art: Two equal lines with different arrow ends, one looking longer.

terms.meaning: An instrument that shows one flat picture to each eye so that the brain sees a solid scene. Charles Wheatstone built the first one in 1838.
terms.example: Old 3D picture viewers use a stereoscope.
terms.art: A wooden viewer with two flat pictures and an eye on each side.

terms.meaning: A spinning card with one picture on the front and another on the back. When it spins fast, the two pictures seem to join into one.
terms.example: A bird on one side and a cage on the other seem to put the bird inside the cage.
terms.art: A round card on two strings with a bird on the front and a cage on the back, and the bird seen inside the cage while the card spins.

explanations.definition: Light travels in straight lines unless something bends it or bounces it. That is why we cannot see round corners, and why shadows have sharp edges.
explanations.description: When you shine a torch through three cards with holes, the light only gets through if the holes line up in a straight row. Move one card a little and the light stops. A sunbeam through a window is a straight stripe. A shadow has a sharp edge because light cannot curve round the thing that blocks it. Light can be bent by water or glass, or bounced by a mirror, but in clear air or an empty space it goes straight. Light is also fast. In one second it could go round the Earth more than seven times. So its straight path looks instant.
examples: A torch beam in a dusty room is a straight line.
You cannot see your friend if she stands behind a wall.
The sharp edge of a shadow on a wall shows that light did not curve round the object.
explanations.art: A torch shining through three aligned cards with holes onto a wall spot, and a second picture with the middle card moved so the light stops.
explanations.context: Before we can understand how light gets into the eye, we need to know how light travels. This card gives the first rule.

explanations.definition: A ray is a straight arrow that shows where a thin beam of light is going. A ray diagram uses rays to show the whole journey of light.
explanations.description: Scientists draw light as straight arrows, called rays. The arrow shows the direction the light is going. To draw how you see a mango, you draw an arrow from the lamp to the mango, and an arrow from the mango to your eye. You use a ruler, because light goes straight. A real beam is wider than a line, and a real lamp sends out light in every direction. A ray is a way of drawing one thin path out of all of them. Ray diagrams help us predict things we have not measured yet, such as where a picture will form.
examples: A drawing of a candle, a mirror and an eye, with straight arrows from the candle to the mirror and the mirror to the eye.
A drawing of the Sun, a tree and a shadow, with arrows from the Sun going past the tree.
A drawing in a physics book of light entering a magnifying glass.
explanations.art: A lamp, a mango and an eye with three straight arrows drawn with a ruler.
explanations.context: Ray diagrams are how scientists draw light. This card explains the drawing.

explanations.concept: Every point of a thing sends rays in all directions
explanations.definition: Every point on a lit thing sends light out in every direction. Only a few of those rays go into any one eye.
explanations.description: Think of the tip of a mango. Sunlight lands on it, and it bounces light in every direction, like a tiny lamp. The same is true of every other point on the mango. A very small share of these rays goes into your eye. But because there are so many points and so much light, your eye gets plenty. This is why everyone in a room can see the mango, from every seat. It is also why a plain white wall does not show a picture of the room. Rays from every point of the room land on every point of the wall and mix. To make a picture, the rays must be sorted.
examples: Everyone in a class can see the same blackboard from different seats.
A white wall lit by a window shows no picture of the window, only brightness.
A single candle flame lights the whole room, because it sends light in every direction.
explanations.art: A mango with rays going out from its top, middle and bottom in all directions, and one eye catching a few of them.
explanations.context: We know light goes straight. This card explains why a plain surface cannot show a picture.

explanations.concept: A hole or a lens sorts the rays into a picture
explanations.definition: A tiny hole lets through only one ray from each point of a thing, so a picture forms. A lens does the same job, but lets in much more light, by bending the rays from each point back together.
explanations.description: Put a card with a tiny hole between a lit window and a screen. Each point of the window sends one thin ray through the hole, to one place on the screen. The rays from the top land at the bottom, and the rays from the bottom land at the top. So the picture is upside down. A pinhole makes a sharp but dim picture, because it lets little light through. A lens is a wide window that bends the rays. All the rays from one point of the window, which spread out, are bent so that they meet again at one point on the screen. That gives a bright and sharp picture. Your eye does exactly this, with the lens inside it and the retina as the screen. In 1604, Johannes Kepler worked out that the picture on the retina is upside down.
examples: A magnifying glass held between a window and a card makes an upside-down picture of the window on the card.
A phone camera has a tiny lens that makes a sharp picture on its sensor.
Your retina holds a small upside-down picture of everything you look at.
explanations.art: A candle, a lens and a screen with an upside-down candle picture, and straight rays from the flame tip bent to meet at one point.
explanations.context: The eye makes a picture on the retina. This card explains how a lens does that.

explanations.definition: The lens inside the eye can change its shape. It gets thicker to focus on near things and thinner to focus on far things.
explanations.description: Your retina is always the same distance from your lens. But a near thing and a far thing need different bending to make a sharp picture on it. So the eye changes the lens. Tiny muscles around the lens squeeze it fatter to look at something close, such as a book. When you look at a far hill, they relax and the lens goes flatter. This takes a moment, which is why things look blurry for a second when you glance from a book to the blackboard. The lens gets stiffer with age. From around the age of 40, many people cannot make it thick enough to focus on near print. They need reading glasses. You will measure this when you find the near point of people of different ages.
examples: You look up from a book to a clock on the wall, and it is blurry for a moment.
A grandparent holds the newspaper at arm's length.
A camera has to move its lens in and out to focus, but the eye changes the lens shape.
explanations.art: A thick rounded lens focusing a near pencil, and a thinner flat lens focusing a far tree, both on the same retina.
explanations.context: A lens bends light. This card explains how the eye adjusts the lens for near and far.

explanations.definition: If the eye's focus lands in front of the retina, far things look blurry. This is short sight. If it lands behind the retina, near things look blurry. This is long sight. Glasses fix both.
explanations.description: In a short-sighted eye, the eyeball is a little too long, or the lens is a little too strong. The rays from far things meet before they reach the retina, and are spreading again by the time they land. Glasses with a lens that spreads light a little, called a concave lens, move the focus back. In a long-sighted eye, the focus lands behind the retina, and a lens that squeezes the light, called a convex lens, moves it forward. Short sight is becoming more common in children in many countries. Studies in several countries suggest that children who spend more time outdoors in daylight are less likely to become short-sighted. Scientists are still working out why. Eye tests at school find who needs glasses.
examples: A child who cannot read the board from the back bench but can read a book easily may be short-sighted.
Reading glasses for older people are convex lenses.
Eye camps and hospitals test for glasses all over India.
explanations.art: Two eyes, one with rays meeting in front of the retina and a glasses lens fixing it, and one with rays meeting behind and a reading lens fixing it.
explanations.context: Sometimes the picture is not sharp. This card explains why, and how glasses help.

explanations.definition: The size a thing looks depends on the angle between the rays from its top and its bottom. A far thing makes a smaller angle, so it looks smaller.
explanations.description: A person stands 4 metres away. Two straight rays go from her head and her feet into your eye. The angle between them is the visual angle. Now she steps back to 8 metres. The rays are still straight, but they come from further away, so the angle is smaller. It is about half as big. So she looks about half as tall. You can check this with a ruler held at arm's length. Because the eye makes a picture on the retina, a smaller angle means a smaller picture. This is also why signs for far readers must be bigger. A sign twice as far away must be twice as tall to look the same size.
examples: A person at 8 metres looks about half the height of the same person at 4 metres.
A road sign for fast drivers has much bigger letters than a notice in a classroom.
The Moon is huge, but looks small, because it is so far.
explanations.art: Two children, one close and one far, with straight lines from their heads and feet to an eye, making a wide angle and a narrow angle.
explanations.context: Things that are far away look small. This card says exactly why.

explanations.definition: Your two eyes are a few centimetres apart, so each sees a slightly different picture. The brain uses the difference to work out how far away things are.
explanations.description: Hold a finger up at arm's length and swap eyes. The finger jumps against the wall behind it. Now bring the finger close to your nose and swap again. It jumps much further. The jump is called parallax. Near things jump a lot, and far things jump a little, so the size of the jump tells the brain the distance. Your brain does this all day, below your notice, for every part of the scene. It works best for things within a few metres, such as a ball coming towards you. For far things, the difference is too small. Scientists call seeing with two eyes binocular vision. Reports suggest that somewhere between 1 person in 20 and 1 in 10 cannot use their two eyes together to judge depth.
examples: Threading a needle is much harder with one eye closed.
A bus window shows parallax: near trees zip by, far hills drift.
Astronomers measure the distance to some stars by looking at them from two places half a year apart.
explanations.art: A child's two eyes seeing a pencil against a wall, with the left view and right view overlapped, and the jump marked.
explanations.context: Your first test is the finger jump. This card explains what the jump is and what it tells the brain.

explanations.definition: Even one eye can judge distance, using clues in the picture and the movement of the head.
explanations.description: A person with sight in only one eye can still judge distance well, using many clues. A near thing looks bigger than the same thing far away. A thing in front of another thing hides part of it, so it must be nearer. Far hills look hazy and bluish. Shadows show shape. And if you move your head a little, near things slide across the view more than far things, which gives the same jump as two eyes, one view after the other. Painters use all these clues, except movement, to make a flat painting look deep. A person with one eye usually learns to use these clues very well. Close one eye and the world does not go flat, but touching the tips of two pencils together gets harder, because the quick difference between two views is missing.
examples: A flat painting of a road that narrows into the distance looks deep.
A person with sight in one eye sways her head slightly to judge a ball's distance.
A far mountain looks blue-grey and hazy, so we know it is far.
explanations.art: A painting of a road with converging lines, a house overlapping a tree, and smaller far hills drawn in haze, with labels for each clue.
explanations.context: You might think depth needs two eyes. This card says what happens when there is only one.

explanations.concept: Hunters and hunted: where the eyes sit
explanations.definition: Hunting animals, such as owls, cats and tigers, have both eyes at the front, which gives depth for a pounce. Hunted animals, such as deer, hens and horses, have eyes at the sides, which gives a wide view.
explanations.description: Eyes at the front see the same scene from two nearby places, so the pictures overlap a lot. That gives strong depth for judging a leap. Eyes at the sides cannot overlap much, but each one sees a different part of the world, so together they see almost all the way round. A horse or a rabbit can watch for danger from nearly every side without turning their head. A hen bobs her head as she walks, which keeps the picture steady for a moment between steps. A chameleon moves each eye separately. Humans have front-facing eyes. One idea is that our early primate ancestors gained them from jumping between branches. Scientists still discuss this. Neither design is better. Each fits the way the animal lives.
examples: An owl turns the whole head to look, because her eyes face the front and cannot move much.
A deer at a waterhole can see a tiger sneaking from the side.
A hen bobs her head as she walks, to keep the picture steady between steps.
explanations.art: A top-down drawing of an owl with two forward wedges of view overlapping, and a deer with two wide side wedges covering almost a full circle.
explanations.context: Different animals put their eyes in different places. This card explains why.

explanations.concept: The sharp spot and the edges
explanations.definition: Only a tiny spot in the middle of the retina, the fovea, sees fine detail. The rest sees blurry shapes, movement and dim light.
explanations.description: Hold your thumb out at arm's length. The sharp part of your vision is about the size of your thumbnail. Everything else is blurry, though the world does not seem that way. Your eyes jump from place to place about three times every second, pointing the sharp spot at one thing after another. Your brain builds a picture that feels sharp everywhere. The edges of your vision have few cone cells and many rod cells, so they notice movement and dim light, but not much colour. That is why you notice a bus coming from the side before you can say its colour. It is also why a faint star seems to vanish when you look straight at it and return when you look a little to the side.
examples: You read by moving your sharp spot along a line of words.
A faint star appears when you look beside it, and disappears when you stare at it.
You see a movement at the edge of your vision before you know what moved.
explanations.art: A person looking at a word with a small bright circle showing the sharp spot, and the surrounding view blurred.
explanations.context: In the last unit, you learned about rods and cones. This card says where they are, and what that means for what you see.

explanations.description: The signals from your eyes take a short time to travel and to be put together by the brain. Scientists think it is about a tenth of a second or more. So what you see is slightly old. A ball moving at 10 metres each second moves a whole metre in that time. Yet fielders catch balls. The brain does not simply report the old picture. It predicts where the ball will be, using what it has learned from many catches. This is why a skilled fielder can catch a ball that she could not possibly have seen in time. There is also an older delay in the light itself. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us, so you see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago. Scientists still argue about how the brain does its predicting.
examples: A fielder runs to where the ball will land, not to where it is.
You see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.
The stars you see tonight are shown as they were years ago, and for some, hundreds of years ago.
explanations.art: A fielder running towards a spot on the ground ahead of a falling ball, with a dotted line to where the ball will land.
explanations.context: What you see seems to be happening right now. This card says that it is slightly old.

explanations.concept: The Moon looks bigger near the horizon
explanations.description: Hold a small lentil or pea at arm's length, in front of the Moon when it is high in the sky. Do the same when the Moon is just above the horizon. The Moon is covered by the same lentil in both. A photograph shows the same size too. Yet to the eye, the Moon near the horizon looks much bigger. This is an illusion, and it has been argued about for more than 2,000 years. Scientists agree that the Moon is not really larger. They do not agree on the reason.
examples: The full Moon rising over the sea at Marina Beach in Chennai looks huge.
The same Moon high overhead looks small.
A photograph shows both at the same size.

perspectives.who: Many vision scientists, following ideas from Ibn al-Haytham about 1,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: The brain thinks the horizon Moon is further away than the high Moon, because there is a lot of ground in between. So it guesses that the horizon Moon must be bigger.
The sky looks like a flattened dome, so the horizon looks further than the top. The brain scales the Moon's size to fit.
No single explanation fits all the tests. Several effects probably work together. The mystery is still open.

explanations.art: The Moon near a row of trees and a house on the horizon looking large, and the Moon high above in empty sky looking small, with a lentil at arm's length covering each.
explanations.context: The Moon looks different sizes at different times. This card gives the main ideas, and says that nobody agrees.

explanations.concept: Why we have a blind spot and an octopus does not
explanations.definition: In the eyes of humans and other backboned animals, the nerve fibres lie in front of the light-catching cells, so the nerve must pass through the retina, which leaves a blind spot. An octopus's retina is wired the other way round, so she has no blind spot.
explanations.description: In your eye, the light has to pass through a layer of nerve fibres before it reaches the light-catching cells. The fibres all gather together and leave the eye in one place, the optic nerve. At that place there are no light-catching cells, which makes the blind spot. In an octopus, the light-catching cells face the light directly, and the nerve fibres lie behind them. So she has no blind spot. Eyes of octopuses and eyes of humans look alike. Scientists think the two designs evolved separately, from far-off ancestors that could only sense light. No design is better in every way. A human brain fills in the blind spot, and we have a fovea. An octopus has no blind spot, and can sense polarised light, which we cannot.
examples: Your eye has a blind spot, and you do not notice it.
An octopus has no blind spot, though her eye looks much like yours.
Two eyes cover for each other's blind spots.
explanations.art: A cutaway human eye with nerve fibres in front of the retina and a blind spot, beside an octopus eye with the nerve fibres behind.
explanations.context: In Class 3, you found your blind spot. This card says why it is there.

explanations.concept: Two pictures that join in the eye
explanations.description: A thaumatrope has a bird on one side of a card and a cage on the other. When you twirl it quickly, the bird seems to be inside the cage. A flip book, a cartoon and a film use the same trick. Pictures shown one after another, quickly enough, seem to join or to move. The old explanation, called persistence of vision, said the eye holds on to each picture for a moment. Many scientists now think that this is only part of the story. The brain also builds movement from a series of still pictures. They still argue about how it does so.
examples: A film shows 24 still pictures every second, and your brain sees smooth movement.
A flip book of a bouncing ball seems to move when you flick the pages.
A ceiling fan seems to slow down or turn backwards in some videos.

perspectives.who: An older explanation, persistence of vision
perspectives.explanation: The eye holds on to each picture for a short moment, so one picture is still there when the next arrives, and the two seem to be seen together.
The brain does not just add pictures. It actively joins nearby pictures, and builds movement between them. The effect called the phi phenomenon was described by Max Wertheimer in 1912.
Both ideas explain part of it. The exact steps in the brain are not yet clear.

explanations.art: A thaumatrope disc spinning, with a bird and a cage joining into a single picture of a bird in a cage.
explanations.context: You will make a card that joins two pictures. This card says what scientists think is going on.

agreed.text: Light travels in straight lines through clear air, and shadows and sunbeams show it.
agreed.evidence: Three cards with holes only let a torch beam through when the holes are in a line, and a shadow has sharp edges.

agreed.text: The eye's lens and cornea make a sharp, upside-down picture on the retina.
agreed.evidence: Kepler worked it out in 1604. Scheiner saw the picture on the back of an eye in the early 1600s. A lens held in front of a window makes the same sort of picture on a card.

agreed.text: The lens changes shape to focus on near and far things, and gets stiffer with age.
agreed.evidence: The near point of the eye moves further away with age, as everyone can measure with a ruler.

agreed.text: Two eyes give two slightly different pictures, and the brain uses the difference to judge depth.
agreed.evidence: In 1838, Wheatstone made flat drawings look solid by showing one to each eye. Touching pencil tips together is harder with one eye covered.

agreed.text: Only a small spot in the middle of the retina sees fine detail.
agreed.evidence: The fovea is packed with cone cells, and this has been seen and counted in the retinas of people.

agreed.text: Animals that hunt tend to have eyes in front, and animals that are hunted tend to have eyes at the sides.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have compared the eye positions and fields of view of hundreds of kinds of animals.

challenging.claim: Light can bend round corners, the way sound does.
challenging.for: We can hear someone talking round a corner, and light is a kind of wave, like sound.
challenging.against: Light waves are extremely tiny, so they bend round edges by only a very small amount, much too small to notice. A shadow has a sharp edge, and we cannot see round a corner. Sound waves are much longer, so they bend round corners easily.

challenging.claim: The picture on the retina is upside down, so the brain must flip it the right way up.
challenging.for: The picture on the retina really is upside down.
challenging.against: There is no screen inside the head where a flipped picture is shown. In the 1890s, George Stratton wore glasses that turned his view upside down. After several days his brain learned to connect what he saw with what he touched, and the world seemed normal again. 'Up' is something the brain learns, not a direction in the retina.

challenging.claim: We have two eyes only so that we have a spare if one is hurt.
challenging.for: People with one eye can manage well, so a spare seems useful.
challenging.against: Two eyes also give us the depth that comes from two views, and a wider field of view. The spare is a bonus, not the main job.

challenging.claim: Reading in dim light damages your eyes.
challenging.for: Reading in dim light makes eyes feel tired and sore.
challenging.against: Eye doctors say that reading in dim light does not harm the eyes for good. It can make them tired, and it is easier to read in good light. The tiredness goes away after rest.

challenging.claim: The Moon really is bigger when it is near the horizon.
challenging.who: Many people who watch it rise.
challenging.for: It looks much bigger, and it looks bigger every time.
challenging.against: A photograph and a lentil held at arm's length show the same size in both places. It is an illusion in the brain.

challenging.claim: Everyone with two healthy eyes sees depth from the difference between them.
challenging.for: Most people with two healthy eyes do.
challenging.against: A small share of people, reported at between 1 in 20 and 1 in 10, cannot use the two views together, even with healthy eyes. They use the other clues for depth, and manage well. Susan Barry, a neuroscientist in the USA, gained this kind of depth sight as an adult, and wrote a book about it.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought we judge how far things are only from clues in a single picture, such as how big a thing looks and what hides what. About 500 years ago, the artist Leonardo da Vinci wrote that a painting can never look as solid as a real scene. But nobody had tested what the two eyes do. In 1838, Charles Wheatstone, a scientist in London, built an instrument called a stereoscope, with two mirrors. He drew two flat pictures of the same shape, each from a slightly different place, and showed one to each eye. The brain joined the two, and the flat drawings suddenly looked solid. Depth did not need a solid thing. The small difference between two views was enough. Clues in a single picture still matter, but the difference between two views is a clue of its own.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Depth comes only from clues in a single picture, such as size and overlap. Wheatstone's two flat drawings, one for each eye, looked solid, which showed that the difference between the views of two eyes is a clue of its own.

big_questions.q: Your two eyes never see the same picture, yet you notice only one. Where do the two pictures become one?
big_questions.hint: Think about the finger jump. Which picture did you see when both eyes were open?

big_questions.q: A person with one eye can catch a ball. If two eyes are not needed, why do we have two?
big_questions.hint: Think about what two eyes make easier, and what one eye does with head movement.

big_questions.q: The picture on your retina is upside down, but the world looks the right way up. Which way up is the world, really?
big_questions.hint: Think about who decides what 'up' means, and what your body feels when you fall.

big_questions.q: A hawk can see a mouse from very far. A hen sees almost all the way round. Which is the better way of seeing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each animal needs to notice to stay alive.

big_questions.q: You see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago. Do you ever see the world as it is right now?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long light takes, and how long your brain takes.

big_questions.q: If your brain builds every picture from signals, how can you be sure the world looks the way it does?
big_questions.hint: Think about what could be checked by touching, measuring or asking someone else.

big_questions.q: The Moon looks big near the horizon and small overhead, but a photo shows the same size. Which one is the real Moon?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a lentil held at arm's length tells you.

big_questions.q: An octopus has no blind spot, and you do. Does that mean her eyes are better than yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each design gives and what each costs.

big_questions.q: Is a thing being 'near' or 'far' a fact about the world, or something each eye works out?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a robot with two cameras does.

big_questions.q: A bat uses sound and an owl uses light to find a mouse in the dark. Do they see the same thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each kind of signal can tell them, and what it cannot.

story.title: Thamarai and the High Catch
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. A person who sees with one eye can judge distance well, using many clues, including how near things shift against far things when the head moves. Two eyes make this easier for things that are close. The beach, the match, Thamarai, Selvam and everyone else in the story are made up.
text: Thamarai was the best fielder on the beach, and half the village still did not believe it.

She was ten. When she was a baby, a bad fever had taken the sight from her left eye. The doctor, a kind woman from Nagercoil, said that her right eye was strong and healthy, and that was all she said. Thamarai did not think about it much. She thought about cricket.

Every evening, when the fishing boats came in, the children of the lane played on the hard sand near the water. They used a taped tennis ball and a flat bat cut from a palmyra branch. The captain was Selvam Anna, who was nineteen and coached the little ones when he came home from college. He was fair, and he was proud of his team.

Thamarai could catch anything. She caught low balls and fast balls and balls that skipped off the sand. But Selvam Anna had read something in a book. "You need two eyes to judge a high catch," he told her kindly. "So I will put you in the corner." And for every big match, he did, where the ball hardly ever came.

On the evening of the Pongal Cup final, the whole beach was full. Their lane was playing the village across the bay. By the last over, the other side needed eight runs to win. The sun hung low over the sea, and the whole sky glowed orange.
The batter was a big girl called Karthika. She swung hard. The ball shot up, higher than the palm trees, and turned into a tiny dark dot against the glare.
Everybody ran. Mythili, the tallest fielder, ran forward, then back, then forward again. She put up her hands, and then she took them down. She had lost the ball in the sun.

Thamarai was standing at the very edge of the beach, where she always stood. She did not run. Instead she did something that made the small children giggle. She swayed her head slowly from side to side, like a hen looking for a grain.

When she was very small, Thamarai had found out a secret. If she held her head still, the world looked flat, like a picture painted on a wall. But when she moved her head a little, near things slid across the view, and far things hardly moved at all. The tall palm on the far dune stayed still. The ball slid. A ball that slid a lot was close. A ball that slid a little was far. No one had taught her this. She had worked it out as a toddler, the way a fisherman learns the sea.
The dark dot slid across the palm tree, quickly. "Close," thought Thamarai, "and coming down fast." She took three steps back. Then one step to the left. She held up both hands.
The ball dropped out of the glare and straight into her hands, as softly as a ripe mango falls from a tree. The other side was out. The Pongal Cup was theirs.
The beach went quiet. Then it exploded. The small ones threw sand in the air.
Later, when the boats were being pulled up the beach, Selvam Anna came and stood beside her. "I read that you need two eyes to judge a high catch," he said slowly. "How did you do it?"
Thamarai shrugged. "Two eyes are better, Anna," she said. "Try this." She held up one finger against the palm tree. "Close your left eye. Now open it, and close the right one."
He did it. His finger leapt sideways against the tree. He did it again. "It jumps," he said.

"It jumps more when you bring it close," said Thamarai. "Two eyes give the brain two views, and the jump tells it how far away something is. I have one eye, so I make my two views myself. One after the other, by moving my head."
Selvam Anna was quiet for a while. Then he laughed, a laugh of surprise. "Then the book was only half right," he said.
From that evening, Thamarai fielded wherever the ball was most likely to go high. And on the first evening of every holiday, Selvam Anna taught the small ones how to find the jump.
story.epiphany: For the parent: to judge how far away something is, the brain uses the small difference between two views. Near things shift more than far things when the view changes. Two eyes give two views at once. A person with one eye can get two views, one after the other, by moving the head. This is the same jump that you see when you swap eyes with a finger held up.
ask: Why does a finger seem to jump sideways when you close one eye and then the other?
Why does a near thing seem to jump more than a far thing when you move your head?
Thamarai moved her head, not her feet. How did that help her to tell where the ball was?
A flat painting of a road can look deep, even though it is flat. What clues could the painter use?

games.title: Seeing Detectives: why can't I see it?
games.context: This is a detective game about seeing. Each card describes someone who cannot see something, or sees something odd. You choose the reason, and a back tells you the right one.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile with the fronts showing, and a set of four reason tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a reason token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a reason.

setup.art: All the tokens turned over together and the reader reading the answer from the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. Then read the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: someone who cannot see, or sees something odd, on the front, and the reason on the back

items.f: A room has no windows. The door is shut tight and the light is off. A girl cannot see her own hand, though her eyes are healthy and wide open.
items.b: NO LIGHT. With no light in the room, no light bounces off her hand into her eyes. Eyes only catch light.

items.f: An explorer's lamp goes out deep in a cave. Her eyes are wide open.
items.b: NO LIGHT. A cave far underground has no light of its own. With her lamp out, there is nothing for her eyes to catch.

items.f: A TV is switched off in a dark room. Its screen looks black.
items.b: NO LIGHT. A switched-off screen makes no light, so almost no light comes from it to the eye.

items.f: A cat sits in a cupboard with the door closed and no light inside. Can she see the mouse beside her?
items.b: NO LIGHT. A cat can see in much dimmer light than we can. But with no light at all, she sees nothing either.

items.f: A shoebox has a sealed lid and a red ball inside. A child looks in through a small peephole.
items.b: NO LIGHT. Nothing lights the ball, so nothing bounces off it into the peephole.

items.f: A mango lies in a dark cupboard. What colour is it?
items.b: NO LIGHT. With no light, nothing bounces off the mango into any eye. No eye can see its colour.

items.f: A torch shines on a toy. A girl holds a book between the toy and her eyes.
items.b: BLOCKED. The toy is still lit, but the light bouncing off it cannot get past the book to her eyes. Light goes in straight lines.

items.f: A friend stands behind a brick wall. You cannot see her face.
items.b: BLOCKED. Light from her face goes straight, and the wall stops it. Light does not bend round the wall.

items.f: In a corridor, you cannot see a person who is walking just round the corner.
items.b: BLOCKED. Light goes in straight lines. The light from the person cannot turn the corner to reach you.

items.f: A cloud covers the Sun, and the field suddenly looks dim.
items.b: BLOCKED. The cloud stops part of the sunlight before it reaches the field, so less light bounces off the field.

items.f: Three cards with holes stand in a row, and a torch spot shows on the wall behind them. A child slides the middle card sideways, and the spot vanishes.
items.b: BLOCKED. Light goes straight, so it only passes through holes that line up. The moved card stops it.

items.f: A hand covers the front of a torch in a dark room, and the room goes dark.
items.b: BLOCKED. The hand stops the light from leaving the torch. The light cannot go round the hand.

items.f: A tiny ant on the far wall cannot be seen from across the room, though the light is good.
items.b: EYE'S LIMIT. From far away the ant makes too small an angle at the eye, so her picture lands on cone cells that cannot tell her from the wall.

items.f: A girl walks from a bright street into a dark cinema. For a minute she can see almost nothing.
items.b: EYE'S LIMIT. Her pupils open quickly, but the rod cells take minutes to become more sensitive. The eyes need time.

items.f: A faint star vanishes when you stare right at it and comes back when you look a little to the side.
items.b: EYE'S LIMIT. The middle of the retina has few of the rod cells that catch dim light. Beside the middle, there are more.

items.f: A red pen is moved in from the side of your view. You see it move before you can say its colour.
items.b: EYE'S LIMIT. The edges of the retina notice movement well, but have few cone cells for colour and detail.

items.f: A child holds a page 3 centimetres from her eyes, and the words are a blur.
items.b: EYE'S LIMIT. The lens cannot get thick enough to focus on a page that close. It is inside her near point.

items.f: A dot on a card vanishes when the card is held at one distance, and returns when the card moves closer.
items.b: EYE'S LIMIT. At that distance its light falls on the blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves the eye and there are no light-catching cells.

items.f: Two lines are exactly the same length. The one with arrow ends pointing outwards looks longer than the one with arrow ends pointing inwards.
items.b: BRAIN'S GUESS. The brain reads the arrow ends as clues to depth and guesses the sizes wrongly.

items.f: The Moon looks huge when it rises over the sea and small when it is high. A photo shows the same size.
items.b: BRAIN'S GUESS. The brain judges the size from clues about distance. Scientists still argue about exactly why.

items.f: A flat drawing of a box, with lines that meet, looks as if it sticks out of the page.
items.b: BRAIN'S GUESS. Lines that meet are a clue to depth, and the brain adds depth to a flat drawing.

items.f: A child sees a face in a cloud.
items.b: BRAIN'S GUESS. The brain is quick to find faces, and sometimes it finds them where there are none.

items.f: A child closes one eye and tries to touch the tips of two pencils together. She misses.
items.b: BRAIN'S GUESS. With one eye, the brain loses the difference between two views, so its guess about distance is worse.

items.f: A spinning card has a bird on one side and a cage on the other. A child sees the bird inside the cage.
items.b: BRAIN'S GUESS. The two pictures come so quickly that the brain joins them into one.

printables.title: 8 reason tokens: two sets of four, NO LIGHT, BLOCKED, EYE'S LIMIT and BRAIN'S GUESS (copy more for 3 or 4 players)

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 reason tokens. Each player needs a set of four tokens: NO LIGHT, BLOCKED, EYE'S LIMIT and BRAIN'S GUESS. With two players, each takes one set. For three or four players, copy the tokens.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the fronts showing. The back is hidden. One player is the reader.
The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. Everyone else picks the reason they think fits best and puts that token face down.
When everyone is ready, turn the tokens over together. Then the reader reads the back aloud.
A player who picked the right token scores 1 point. A player who also says in one sentence why the reason fits scores 1 more point.
The next player to the left becomes the reader. In a game for two, you take turns to be the reader.
When the cards run out, count the points. The player with the most points wins. If two players have the same, they share the win.
If nobody picked the right reason, the reader reads the back again, and the group talks about why before the next card.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the fronts showing. Give each player a set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card has someone who cannot see something, or sees something odd. You choose a reason. No light. Blocked. Eye's limit. Or the brain's guess.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Seeing Detectives. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first three cards slowly. After each card, read the back aloud and talk about it before you go on.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone chooses a token. Turn them over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who chose right? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What is the difference between NO LIGHT and BLOCKED?
good: With no light, nothing is lit at all.
With blocked light, there is light, but something is in the way.
Blocked means light goes straight and cannot go round.

check.q: A friend stands behind a wall and you cannot see her face. Which reason fits best?
options: Blocked
No light
The brain's guess
check.why: There is plenty of light in the room. But light goes in straight lines, and the wall is in the way. Picking 'no light' mixes up light that is missing with light that is stopped.

flow.context: In this step, you play three practice cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next cards until you have played about twelve in all. The reader reads the back each time. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Your turn to be a detective. Pick your reason. Say why in one sentence. Turn them over. Then listen to the back.
flow.kid: Read the card. Pick a reason. Say why. Turn it over. Score a point.
flow.parent: Some cards have a clear 'eye' part and a 'brain' part. Accept one sentence that gives the idea, even in different words. If a card is hard, such as the Moon at the horizon, say it is a real puzzle and scientists argue about it.

check.q: A faint star vanishes when you stare right at it, and comes back when you look to the side. Which reason fits best?
options: Eye's limit
Blocked
No light
check.why: The star's light is still reaching the eye. The middle of the retina has few of the rod cells that work best in dim light. Beside the middle there are more. So the limit is in the eye.

flow.context: In this step, you play most of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last cards. Count the points. Find out who won.
flow.say: Last cards! Then count your points. Who won?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and count the points.

flow.do: Sit together and ask the question below. Do not give the answer. Let each person say what they think.
flow.say: Look back at the cards. Which kind of reason came up most? Which one was the hardest to tell from the others?
flow.kid: Which reason came up most? Which was hardest to tell apart?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. Each of the four is a different link in a chain. The light must exist, it must travel without being blocked, the eye must be able to catch it, and the brain must make sense of it.
flow.think: Seeing needs light, a clear path, a working eye and a brain. If any one is missing, what happens?
flow.context: This is the last step of Seeing Detectives. You think about how the four reasons differ.

items.p: A torch shines through three cards with holes, and a spot shows on the wall. The spot vanishes when the middle card is slid sideways. What does this show?
opts: Light travels in straight lines
Light bends round the edge of a hole
The torch is weak
items.why: The light only passed through while the three holes were on one straight line. When the middle hole moved off the line, the card blocked the light. Light did not bend round the edge. Picking 'the torch is weak' does not fit, because the spot returns when the card is slid back.

items.p: A shadow has a sharp edge because light cannot curve round the thing that blocks it.
items.why: True. Light goes in straight lines, so the place behind the thing gets no light, and the edge between light and dark is sharp.

items.p: A straight arrow that shows the path of a thin beam of light is called a ____.
items.why: A ray is a drawing of one thin path of light. A ray diagram uses several rays to show a whole journey of light.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how a lens makes a picture of a window on a card.
items: The lens bends the rays that reach it
Rays leave each point of the window in all directions
A small upside-down picture of the window appears on the card
Rays from each point of the window meet again at one point on the card
items.a: order shown
items.why: Light first spreads out from every point of the window. The lens catches some of it and bends it. The rays from each point come together again on the card, and that makes a sharp, upside-down picture.

items.p: Why is the picture on the retina upside down?
opts: The lens bends rays from the top of a thing downwards and rays from the bottom upwards, so they cross
The eye is hung upside down
The brain turns it over before it reaches the eye
items.why: Rays from the top of a thing cross the rays from the bottom as they pass through the lens. So the top ends up at the bottom of the picture. Picking 'the brain turns it over' mixes up the order. The picture is upside down before it gets to the brain.

items.p: You look up from a book to a clock on the wall, and for a moment it is blurry. What is your eye doing?
opts: Changing the lens from thick to thinner
Changing the retina from thin to thick
Making the pupil bigger
items.why: For a near book, the lens is thick. For a far clock, it has to become thinner. This takes a moment, and in that moment the picture is blurry.

items.p: To focus on a near thing, the lens in the eye gets ____.
items.why: A thicker lens bends light more, which is what a near thing needs to make a sharp picture on the retina.

items.p: A friend looks 18 centimetres tall on a ruler held at arm's length when she stands 4 metres away. About how tall will she look when she stands 8 metres away?
opts: About 9 centimetres
About 36 centimetres
About 18 centimetres
items.why: Twice as far away makes the angle at the eye half as big. So she looks about half as tall, which is 9 centimetres. Picking 18 forgets that distance matters. Picking 36 gets the pattern backwards.

items.p: Match each animal to the place where their eyes sit and what that gives.
pairs: eyes at the front, for depth to judge a pounce
eyes at the sides, for a wide view
eyes at the sides, with a head bob to keep the picture steady
each eye can move on its own
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each design suits the way the animal lives. Front eyes give depth for a hunter. Side eyes give a wide view for an animal that must watch for danger.

items.p: When you swapped eyes, a pencil held near jumped much more than a pencil held far. What does the brain use the size of the jump for?
opts: To work out how far away the pencil is
To make the pencil move
To change the colour of the pencil
items.why: A near thing jumps a lot and a far thing jumps a little. So the size of the jump is a clue to the distance.

items.p: A person with sight in only one eye cannot tell how far away anything is.
items.why: False. A person with one eye can use clues such as size, overlap, haze and how things shift when the head moves. Two eyes make it easier for things that are close.

items.p: In the Near Pencil, Far Pencil test, touching the pencil tips together was harder with one eye closed. Explain why in two or three sentences.
items.a: With two eyes, the brain compares two views, and the difference tells it how far apart the tips are. With one eye, that clue is missing. The brain has to guess the gap, and the guess is not as good.
items.why: A strong answer says that two eyes give two views and the difference helps with judging distance. It says what is missing with one eye.

items.p: Draw a ray diagram of a lamp, a mango and an eye. Use a ruler and draw straight arrows to show how you see the mango.
items.a: One arrow goes from the lamp to the mango. Another arrow goes from the mango into the eye. Both arrows are straight and point the way the light travels.
items.why: Light starts at the lamp, bounces off the mango and goes into the eye. No arrow starts in the eye.
items.art: A blank page with a lamp, a mango and an eye drawn in a row.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one help the brain to judge distance with one eye, or does it need two eyes?
items: a nearer tree looks bigger than the same tree far away
a house hides part of the hill behind it
far hills look hazy and blue
a pencil seems to jump when you swap eyes
a near tree slides further than a far tree when you move your head
each eye gets a slightly different picture
items.a: see items
items.why: The first, second, third and fifth are clues in one view, or in one eye's moving view. The jump and the two different pictures only exist when there are two eyes.

items.p: An octopus has no blind spot. Why?
opts: Her light-catching cells face the light and her nerve fibres lie behind them
She has more eyes than we do
Her brain is bigger than ours
items.why: In our eyes, the nerve fibres lie in front of the light-catching cells, so the nerve must pass through the retina. That makes a gap. In an octopus's eye the fibres lie behind, so there is no gap.

items.p: A friend says, 'Light can bend round a corner like sound can, because I can hear my mother in the next room.' Write two sentences to help your friend.
items.a: Sound waves are long, so they bend round corners easily. Light waves are tiny, so they bend round corners by almost nothing, and we cannot see round a corner. A shadow has a sharp edge for the same reason.
items.why: A strong answer says that light goes in straight lines in everyday life, and gives evidence such as sharp shadows or the spot that vanished in the three cards test.

worksheets.title: How the Eye and Brain Build the Picture (stretch)

items.p: Light from a window lands on a plain white wall, but the wall shows no picture of the window. Why?
opts: Rays from every point of the window land on every point of the wall and mix
The wall is too white
Light cannot make pictures
items.why: Each point of the window sends rays in all directions, so every point of the wall gets light from every point of the window. It all mixes. To make a picture, you need a hole or a lens to sort the rays.

items.p: A pinhole and a lens both make a sharp picture. Why is the lens picture much brighter?
opts: The lens gathers light from a wide area and bends it to the same place
The lens makes its own light
The pinhole makes the picture darker on purpose
items.why: A pinhole lets through only a thin beam from each point. A lens is a wide window that bends many rays from each point back together.

items.p: There is a small screen inside the head where a picture is turned right way up and shown.
items.why: False. There is no screen inside the head. The picture on the retina is upside down, but the brain does not need to turn it. It learns how signals from each part of the retina match what we touch and where up is.

items.p: Glasses for a short-sighted eye have a lens that is thinner in the middle, called a ____ lens.
items.why: A concave lens spreads the rays a little, which moves the focus back on to the retina.

items.p: A grandparent holds a newspaper at arm's length to read. What is the most likely reason?
opts: Her lens has become stiffer and cannot get thick enough to focus on near print
Her eyes make weaker rays
The print is smaller than it used to be
items.why: The lens gets stiffer with age. So the near point moves further away. Reading glasses add a lens to help.

items.p: Astronomers can find the distance to some nearby stars by looking at them from two places half a year apart. Explain how this is like the finger jump.
items.a: A near star seems to shift a little against the far stars when the view changes, like a near finger jumps against the wall. The bigger the shift, the nearer the star. The two places half a year apart are like two eyes.
items.why: A strong answer links the idea of two viewpoints, a shift against the background, and distance. Nearer things shift more.

items.p: The Moon looks bigger near the horizon. People disagree about why.

views.says: The brain thinks the horizon Moon is further away, because there is ground in between, so it guesses that the Moon must be bigger.
Several effects probably work together. No single idea explains all the tests.

items.ask: Which view do you find more convincing? Use one fact from this unit. Then say what the other view has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses a fact. For example: a lentil at arm's length covers the Moon in both places, so the Moon is the same size and the difference is in the brain. It then gives the other view a fair point.
items.why: Scientists still do not agree. What everyone accepts is that the Moon does not change size. Both views try to say why the brain guesses wrongly.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the tiny spot of finest detail in the retina
the closest distance at which a thing is still sharp
a near thing seems to shift more than a far thing
how much you can see at once
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four ideas appear all through the unit. The fovea sees detail, the near point shows how far the lens can thicken, parallax gives depth, and the field of view tells how wide you can see.

items.p: A fielder runs to where a ball will land, not to where it is. What does this show?
opts: The brain predicts, because what it sees is a little old
The fielder sees the future
The ball is slow
items.why: Signals from the eye take a short time to be used. A fast ball moves a long way in that time. So the brain predicts where the ball will be.

items.p: Reading in dim light damages your eyes for good.
items.why: False. Reading in dim light can make eyes tired, but eye doctors say it does not cause lasting harm.

items.p: Draw a candle, a lens and a white card. Show rays from the tip of the flame crossing at the lens and meeting on the card. Show how the picture on the card is upside down.
items.a: Rays from the flame tip spread out, pass through the lens and cross, and meet at a point at the bottom of the card. The picture of the flame is upside down.
items.why: The lens bends rays from each point to meet again at one point. Rays from the top cross over the rays from the bottom.
items.art: A blank page with a candle on the left, a lens in the middle and a white card on the right.

items.p: Explain why a sign that is twice as far away must be twice as tall to look the same size. Use the word 'angle'.
items.a: The size a thing looks depends on the angle between the rays from its top and its bottom. Twice as far makes the angle half as big. A sign twice as tall makes the angle twice as big again, so the two cancel and the sign looks the same size.
items.why: A strong answer links distance, size and angle in one chain of reasoning.

items.p: A deer has eyes at the sides of her head. What does she gain?
opts: A very wide view, almost all the way round
Strong depth for a pounce
Better sight in the dark than every other animal
items.why: Side eyes cover different parts of the world, so together they see almost all the way round. That helps a deer spot danger.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one about the sharp centre of the eye, or about the edges of the retina?
items: notices a movement from the side
makes a faint star seem to appear when you look beside it
items.a: see items
items.why: The fovea in the centre has many cone cells, so it sees detail and colour. The edges have many rod cells, so they are good at movement and dim light.

items.p: Put these in order, from the nearest near point to the furthest.
items.a: order shown
items.why: The lens gets stiffer with age. A child can focus very close, an adult in the forties less close, and an older person only at a greater distance.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A hen, a deer, a horse, an owl. Say why.
items.a: an owl
items.why: The hen, the deer and the horse have eyes at the sides of the head, for a wide view. The owl has both eyes at the front, for depth.

items.p: A rabbit has eyes at the sides of her head. Why can she not judge the distance of a close object as well as a cat?
opts: Her two eyes see mostly different parts of the world, so there is little overlap to compare
Her eyes are too small
Rabbits cannot see close things
items.why: Depth from two eyes needs overlapping views. Side eyes overlap very little, so there is not much difference to measure.

items.p: In 1838, Charles Wheatstone showed two flat drawings, one to each eye, that looked solid. What did this show?
opts: The difference between the views of the two eyes is a clue to depth in itself
The brain draws solid things
Flat things are really solid
items.why: The drawings were flat, so they had no real depth. Yet the brain made a solid scene from the small difference between them.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether children catch a ball better with two eyes open than with one eye covered. Say what you change, what you keep the same, and how you will count.
items.a: I change whether one eye or two eyes are open. I keep the ball, the distance, the thrower and the number of throws the same. I toss 10 times with two eyes and 10 times with one, in a mixed order so that practice does not help one side. I count how many catches.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, repeats the test and counts the results. It also mixes the order, so that practice does not give one side an unfair help.

items.p: A scientist wants to check that the picture on a retina is upside down. Which test would work?
opts: Take the back off an animal's eye so that the retina shows through, and look at the picture
Ask a person to draw what they see
Shine a torch into the eye
items.why: Looking at the picture on the retina directly is the best test. Scheiner did this in the early 1600s. Asking someone what they see would not show the picture on the retina, because the brain has already worked on it.

items.p: Light from a star takes the same time to reach us as light from the Moon.
items.why: False. Light from the Moon takes about a second. Light from the nearest stars takes years. We see stars as they were long ago.

items.p: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. What does this mean for what you see?
opts: You see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago
You see the Sun as it is now
The Sun is only 8 minutes old
items.why: Light takes time to travel. So the picture of the Sun that reaches your eye left it about 8 minutes before.

items.p: The shift of a nearby star against far stars, when seen from two places half a year apart, is called ____.
items.why: Parallax is the shift in the position of a thing when you change your view. Nearer things shift more.

items.p: A hit ball moves 10 metres in one second, and the signals from the eye take about a tenth of a second to be used. How far does the ball move in that time? Why must a fielder predict where the ball will land?
items.a: In one tenth of a second the ball moves 1 metre. The picture the brain is using is already 1 metre behind. The fielder cannot wait for the picture, so she must predict where the ball will be.
items.why: A strong answer divides 10 metres by 10 to get 1 metre, and says that the brain's picture is a little old, so it has to predict.

items.p: Why is short sight becoming more common in children? Scientists are still working it out.

views.says: Children now spend more time on close work such as reading and screens, which may strain the eye as it grows.
Children now spend less time outdoors in daylight, and daylight may help the eye to grow the right shape.

items.ask: Which idea do you find more convincing? What test could help to settle it? Then say what the other idea has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks an idea and plans a test, such as comparing children who spend different amounts of time outdoors, or following children over years. It gives the other idea a fair point. Both could be true.
items.why: Scientists have not settled this. Studies in several countries suggest that time outdoors helps, but the reason is unclear.

items.p: A cat jumps on a mouse. Why do both her eyes face the front?
opts: Two overlapping views give her strong depth for judging the leap
Eyes at the front see further than eyes at the sides
She can see in the dark that way
items.why: Overlapping views let the brain compare and measure the distance. This is what a hunter needs for a leap.

items.p: Sort these. Do scientists agree on it, or does nobody know yet?
items: Two eyes give two slightly different pictures.
The brain uses the difference to judge depth.
Light travels in straight lines in clear air.
Exactly why the Moon looks bigger near the horizon.
How the brain turns signals into the experience of a solid world.
items.a: see items
items.why: The first three have been tested many times. The reason for the Moon illusion is argued about, and how signals become an experience is still an open question.

items.p: A robot car uses two cameras to measure distance. Explain how this is like what your eyes do.
items.a: The two cameras see the same scene from two places, a little apart, like two eyes. A near thing is at different places in the two pictures, and a far thing is at nearly the same place. The robot measures the difference and works out the distance.
items.why: A strong answer says that the cameras compare two views and measure the shift. Nearer things shift more.

items.p: A spinning thaumatrope seems to show a bird inside a cage. Which statement fits best?
opts: The brain joins two pictures that come very quickly one after the other
The bird and the cage are drawn on the same side
The card makes a new picture of its own
items.why: The card shows the bird and the cage one after the other, many times a second. Your brain joins them. Scientists still discuss exactly how.

items.p: Draw a top-down picture of a head with two eyes looking at a pencil held in front, with a wall behind. Draw the line of sight from each eye to the pencil and on to the wall. Mark where the pencil seems to be on the wall for each eye.
items.a: Two lines start at the two eyes and meet at the pencil. They carry on to the wall and land at two different places. The distance between the two places is the jump.
items.why: The two eyes see the pencil against different parts of the wall. The distance between those parts is the jump.
items.art: A blank page with a top-down head with two eyes on the left, a pencil in the middle and a wall on the right.

items.p: Label the drawing of an eye: cornea, lens, retina, fovea, blind spot and optic nerve.
items.a: The cornea is the clear window at the front, the lens is behind the pupil, the retina lines the back, the fovea is the tiny sharp spot in the middle of the retina, the blind spot is where the nerve leaves, and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.
items.why: Light passes through the cornea and lens and lands on the retina. The fovea sees fine detail. The blind spot has no light-catching cells.
items.art: A cutaway drawing of a human eye with unlabelled parts and pointers.

items.p: A child cannot read the board from the back bench but reads a book easily. What may help?
opts: An eye test, and perhaps glasses with a concave lens
Sitting closer to the Sun
Eating more carrots
items.why: This is a sign of short sight. A concave lens spreads the light a little, and moves the focus back on to the retina.

experiments.title: Three Cards, Three Holes: can light go round a corner?
experiments.question: A torch shines through three cards with holes. If we slide the middle card a little to the side, does the light still reach the wall? Can light go round a corner?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will happen to the spot of light on the wall when the middle card is moved a little? Can light bend round the edge of a hole? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same three cards, the same torch and the same wall. Keep the torch at the same place and pointing the same way each time. Change only one thing: how far the middle card is moved sideways. Use the ruler to measure each shift, and look at the spot for a few seconds each time.
results_table: How far the middle card is moved sideways (mm)
Spot of light on the wall (bright, dim or none)
A bendy straw at the elbow: can I see the lamp? (yes or no)

materials.item: 3 pieces of stiff card, each about 10 centimetres by 15 centimetres (postcards, or cut from an old cereal box)
a hole punch, or a sharp pencil, to make a hole about 5 millimetres wide in each card (a grown-up does this)
3 lumps of clay or atta dough to stand the cards up
a torch, or a phone torch, resting on a book
a ruler
a plain wall or a white card to catch the spot of light, in a room you can make dim
a bendy drinking straw and a straight stiff straw (or a rolled paper tube)
a lit lamp or a bright window (not showing the Sun) to look at through the straws
a piece of wool about 1 metre long (optional)
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes, because a hole punch or a pencil point can slip. Never look at the Sun through the holes or the straws.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three cards in a row with the torch and the spot of light. Draw them again with the middle card moved, and draw where the light stops.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you stand three cards with holes in a row and shine a torch through them. You find out whether the light goes in a straight line or can go round a corner.

setup.art: Three cards, each with a round hole 5 centimetres from the bottom, lying on a table with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make a hole at the same height in each card.

setup.art: Three cards standing in clay lumps in a row, 20 centimetres apart, with their holes in a line and a torch pointing along the line.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the cards in a row with the holes lined up. Put the torch behind the first card.

setup.art: A small bright spot of light on a wall at the end of the row of cards, in a dim room.
setup.caption: 3. Look for a small spot of light on the wall.

setup.art: The middle card slid sideways by a few millimetres with a ruler, and no spot on the wall.
setup.caption: 4. Slide the middle card sideways bit by bit. Watch the spot.

setup.art: A child looking through a straight straw at a lamp and seeing it, and then through a bent straw and seeing nothing.
setup.caption: 5. Look at a lamp through a straight straw and then a bent straw.

flow.do: Show your child the cards, the torch and the clay. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will shine a torch through three cards with holes. Then we will slide the middle card a little to the side. What will happen to the light on the wall? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A torch shines through three holes. We slide the middle card sideways. What happens to the light? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the spot when the middle card is moved a little?
good: It will still be there, because light bends round the edge of the hole.
It will vanish, because light goes in a straight line.
It will get dimmer.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Some children think light will curve round the hole, as sound does round a corner. That is a good idea to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three Cards test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Mark a point 5 centimetres up from the bottom in the middle of each card. A grown-up makes a hole of about 5 millimetres at each mark. Stand each card up in a lump of clay.
flow.say: Mark the same height on each card. A grown-up makes a hole at each mark. Then we stand the cards up in clay.
flow.kid: Mark 5 centimetres up on each card. A grown-up makes the holes. Stand the cards in clay.
flow.parent: The three holes must be at exactly the same height. Measure from the bottom of each card, not by eye. Holes much bigger than a pencil make the test harder to read. A hole punch makes a bigger hole, about 6 millimetres. That works too. Use thick card, such as a cereal box, or two layers of thin card. A phone torch is bright enough to glow through thin white card, which would spoil the test.

check.q: Why must the three holes be at exactly the same height?
options: So that a straight line can pass through all three holes
So that the cards look neat
Because light needs big holes
check.why: If light goes in a straight line, it can only pass through three holes if they are all on one line. If the holes are at different heights, we could not tell whether the light bent or the holes were off. Picking 'neat' is about looks. This test is about the path of light.

flow.context: In this step, you make the three cards and stand them up.

flow.do: Stand the cards in a row, 20 centimetres apart, with the holes in a line. Rest the torch on a book behind the first card, pointing along the line. Dim the room. Look for a spot of light on the wall.
flow.say: Line up the three cards. Put the torch behind the first card, pointing straight along the holes. Make the room dim. Can you see a spot of light on the wall?
flow.kid: Line up the cards. Point the torch through the holes. Look for a spot on the wall.
flow.parent: Keep the torch steady and aimed right at the first hole, with the torch about 5 centimetres from it, so that little light leaks round the card. The spot on the wall is small and bright. If you see no spot, check that the holes are on one line and the torch points along it. For an extra check, thread the wool through all three holes and pull it tight. When the holes line up, the wool is straight. It will bend if a card is moved. Put the wool away before the next step.

chart.title: Made-up example: how a filled-in table can look
cols: Bendy straw: can I see the lamp?

flow.context: In this step, you line up the cards and see the spot of light on the wall.

flow.do: Slide the middle card sideways by 2 millimetres. Look at the spot. Then slide it 4, 6, 8 and 10 millimetres. Use the ruler to measure each shift. Write what the spot does each time.
flow.say: Slide the middle card sideways. Two millimetres first. Look at the spot. Then four. Then six. What happens to the light?
flow.kid: Slide the middle card a little. Look at the spot. Slide it more. What happens?
flow.parent: Typically the spot dims at about 3 to 5 millimetres and vanishes by about 6 to 10 millimetres. It depends on the hole size and the torch, so write what you really see. A little light may leak at the edges. That is normal and still shows that light does not go round the card. If the spot never vanishes, the holes are too big or the torch is too wide: make smaller holes, or move the torch right up to the first card. Roles for 2 to 4 children: one holds the torch, one slides the middle card, one reads the ruler, one writes the table. Swap roles for each shift, and let every child look at the spot. One child alone with a parent: the child slides and looks, the parent reads the ruler and writes.

check.q: The spot vanished when the middle card was slid a few millimetres. What does this show?
options: Light goes in a straight line, and the moved card now blocks the line
Light gets tired after 20 centimetres
The torch ran out of battery
check.why: The light went through the first hole in a straight line. When the middle hole was no longer on the line, the card blocked the light. It did not bend round the edge of the hole. Picking 'tired' or 'battery' does not fit, because the spot returns as soon as you slide the card back.
