flow.context: In this step, you move the middle card in small steps and watch the spot.

flow.do: Look at a lit lamp or a bright window across the room, but never at the Sun, through a straight straw. Then bend the straw at the elbow and look again. Write what you see each time.
flow.say: Look through a straight straw at the lamp. Can you see it? Now bend the straw in the middle and look again. What happens?
flow.kid: Look at a lamp through a straight straw. Then bend the straw. What do you see?
flow.parent: Through the straight straw, the lamp is easy to see. When the straw is bent sharply, you see only the dark inside of the straw. The light cannot turn the bend. A rolled paper tube that you bend gives the same result. Each child needs a clean straw of their own, or wash the end first. Use a lamp or a bright window, never the Sun.
flow.context: In this step, you look through a straight straw and a bent straw.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about how light travels? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: light goes in straight lines and does not go round corners. What I saw: the spot vanished when the middle card was moved a few millimetres, and the bent straw showed no lamp. Why: the light could only pass if the holes were on one straight line.
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: Near Pencil, Far Pencil: the finger jump and the depth test
experiments.question: When we swap eyes, a pencil seems to jump sideways against a wall. Does the jump depend on how far the pencil is from our eyes? And is it harder to judge distance with one eye?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When you swap eyes, will a pencil held close jump more or less than a pencil held far? Will it be easier or harder to touch two pencil tips together with one eye closed? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Sit on the same chair, at the same distance from the strip on the wall. Hold the pencil still with your elbow on a table or against your side. Change only one thing at a time: first the distance of the pencil from your eyes, and then whether one eye or two eyes are open. Do each measurement twice, and use the middle of the two numbers if they differ.
results_table: Pencil held this far from my eyes
Number on the strip with only my left eye open
Number with only my right eye open

materials.item: a strip of paper about 1 metre long, taped to a wall at eye height, with a mark every 5 centimetres and a big number, about 4 centimetres tall, every 10 centimetres from 0 to 100 (draw it with a ruler and a thick pen)
tape to stick the strip to the wall
2 pencils with blunt tips (not freshly sharpened)
a chair placed 2 metres from the wall (about 4 big steps), and a table to rest your elbow on
a helper to write down the numbers that you call out
a ruler to check the pencil's distance from your eyes
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use blunt pencils and keep the tips well away from faces and eyes. Move the pencils slowly, and keep the nearest pencil at least a hand-span from the nose. A grown-up stays close by.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Count the pencil tips that touched with both eyes and with one eye, and draw a bar chart with one bar for each. Write how many centimetres the jump changed as the pencil got nearer.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you swap eyes while holding a pencil at three distances, and measure how far it seems to jump against a strip on the wall. Then you try to touch two pencil tips together with one eye and with two.

setup.art: A paper strip with numbers from 0 to 100 taped to a wall at eye height, and a chair two metres away.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the number strip to the wall. Put the chair 2 metres away.

setup.art: A child with her left eye closed, holding a pencil in front of the number strip, and a helper reading a number.
setup.caption: 2. Close one eye. Line up the pencil with a number. Call it out. The helper writes it.

setup.art: The same child with the other eye closed, and the pencil now seeming to be at a different number.
setup.caption: 3. Swap eyes. The pencil seems to jump to another number.

setup.art: A child holding one pencil in each hand with the tips almost touching, with one eye closed and the other open.
setup.caption: 4. Try to touch two pencil tips together, with one eye closed.

flow.do: Show your child the strip, the pencils and the chair. Ask for a guess and a reason for each question. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will hold a pencil in front of a strip on the wall and swap eyes. Does a close pencil jump more or less than a far pencil? And is it harder to touch two pencils with one eye? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Swap eyes with a pencil. Does a close pencil jump more or less than a far one? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the pencil when you swap eyes?
good: It will stay in the same place.
It will jump sideways.
A close pencil will jump more.

ask.q: Why do you think touching the tips might be harder with one eye?
good: With one eye, I cannot tell how far away the tips are.
Two eyes give a better view.
I think it will be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write what they say.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Near Pencil, Far Pencil test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Tape the number strip to the wall at your child's eye height. Place the chair 2 metres from the wall. Practise swapping eyes with a finger held up at arm's length, before you use a pencil.
flow.say: Put the strip on the wall. Sit on the chair. Hold up a finger and swap eyes a few times. What do you see the finger do?
flow.kid: Sit on the chair. Hold up a finger. Swap eyes. What do you see?
flow.parent: Eye height means the level of your child's eyes when she sits. Draw the numbers big enough to read from 2 metres away. Swap by closing one eye and opening the other. Do not move the head.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the strip and practise swapping eyes.

flow.do: Hold the pencil upright at arm's length, in front of the strip. Close your right eye. Call out the number on the strip that the pencil seems to cover. The helper writes it down. Swap eyes and call out the number again. Write both numbers and the jump. Repeat with the pencil half as far, and again a hand-span from your nose.
flow.say: Hold the pencil up at arm's length. Close your right eye. What number does it cover? Now swap. What number now? Then bring the pencil nearer and do it again.
flow.kid: Hold the pencil up. Swap eyes. Read the two numbers. Bring the pencil nearer. Do it again.
flow.parent: Only the child can say which number the pencil covers, because it depends on where her eyes are. The helper must not read it from the side. For a child with eyes about 5.5 centimetres apart, with the strip 2 metres away, typical jumps are about 15 centimetres at arm's length, about 35 centimetres at half arm's length, and 60 to 80 centimetres a hand-span from the nose, which may be off the strip (then write 'off the strip', and use a shorter distance). Your numbers will differ. The pattern matters: the nearer the pencil, the bigger the jump. If your child cannot focus on the pencil at the nearest distance, use a bit further, and say so. Children with eyes further apart usually get bigger jumps, so compare two children and ask why. For 2 to 4 children: each child fills in their own table, one at a time, while the others write down the numbers and check the distance with the ruler. For one child with a parent: the parent writes and checks the distance.

check.q: The pencil jumped further the nearer it was held. What does the brain do with the size of the jump?
options: It uses the jump to work out how far away the pencil is
It ignores the jump
It uses the jump to move the pencil
check.why: Near things jump a lot and far things jump a little, so the size of the jump tells the brain the distance. Picking 'ignores the jump' cannot be right, because people judge distance well with two eyes. Picking 'move the pencil' mixes up what the eyes see with what the pencil does.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table
cols: Pencil held this far from my eyes

flow.context: In this step, you measure the jump of a pencil at three distances.

flow.do: Hold a pencil in each hand at arm's length. Point the tips at each other, with a gap of about 20 centimetres. Bring the tips together in one smooth move. The tips must meet head-on, not slide past or hit the sides. Try 10 times with both eyes open. Then try 10 times with one eye closed. Count the times the tips touched.
flow.say: Hold two pencils with the tips pointing at each other. Bring them together in one smooth move. Do you touch? Try ten times with two eyes. Then ten times with one eye shut.
flow.kid: Hold two pencils tip to tip. Bring them together in one move. Ten tries with two eyes. Ten with one.
flow.parent: With both eyes, most children touch 8 to 10 times out of 10. With one eye, often 2 to 6 times. Some children do well with one eye. That is a real result too, because they judge the gap from other clues. Do not move the head during the test, so the comparison is fair.

check.q: With one eye closed, the pencil tips often passed each other. Why?
options: The brain loses the difference between two views that tells it how far away the tips are
One eye cannot see a pencil
The pencil moved on its own
check.why: With two eyes, the brain has two views to compare, and the difference tells it how far apart the tips are. With one eye, that clue is gone, so judging a small gap is harder. Picking 'one eye cannot see a pencil' is not right, because the closed-eye pencils were still seen. Only the distance was harder to judge.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many tries out of 10 touched

flow.context: In this step, you try to touch two pencil tips with two eyes and with one eye.

flow.do: Look at your guesses and your results together. Ask your child to say three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about two eyes? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: two eyes help the brain to judge how far away things are. What I saw: the nearer pencil jumped more, and touching the pencil tips was harder with one eye. Why: the two eyes see from different places, and the brain uses the difference.
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: A Lens Makes a Window Picture: where is the sharp place?
experiments.question: Can a lens make a picture of a window on a card? And does the card have to move when the bright thing is nearer?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you hold a magnifying glass between a bright window and a white card, what will you see on the card? Will it be the right way up or upside down? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same lens, the same card and the same dim room each time. Keep the lens pointing at the bright thing. Change only one thing: how far the bright thing is from the lens. Measure from the lens to the card when the picture is sharpest. Measure twice.
results_table: How far it is from the lens
How far the card is from the lens when the picture is sharp
Upside down or right way up?

materials.item: a magnifying glass, or the lens from a pair of reading glasses (a lens that is thicker in the middle)
a sheet of white card about the size of a postcard
a book or a lump of clay to hold the card upright
a ruler or a measuring tape
a room with a window that does not show the Sun, with the curtains drawn on the other windows, or a bright lamp across the room
a phone with the screen at full brightness, showing a plain white page with a big black letter F, standing up as a bright thing that is nearer (a phone torch alone gives only a bright dot)
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never point the lens at the Sun. A lens can focus sunlight into a tiny hot spot that can burn skin, damage eyes and set paper alight. Use a window that does not show the Sun, or a lamp.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the picture of the window that you saw on the card, and mark which way up it is.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you use a magnifying glass to make a picture of a window on a white card. You find out which way up the picture is, and how the sharp place moves.

setup.art: A dim room with one bright window on the far wall, and a child holding a magnifying glass above a white card propped on a book.
setup.caption: 1. Dim the room. Hold the lens between the window and the card.

setup.art: A small sharp upside-down picture of the window, with its frame and a tree, on the white card.
setup.caption: 2. Move the card slowly until a sharp picture of the window appears.

setup.art: A ruler measuring from the lens down to the card.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the distance from the lens to the card.

setup.art: A phone showing a big black letter F on a white screen, standing 50 centimetres from the lens, with a small upside-down F on the card at a slightly larger distance.
setup.caption: 4. Try a bright thing that is nearer. Move the card until the picture is sharp.

flow.do: Show your child the lens, the card and the window. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will hold a magnifying glass between a bright window and a white card. What do you think we will see on the card? Will it be upside down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A lens, a card and a window. What will you see on the card? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which way up do you think the picture will be?
good: The right way up, like the window.
Upside down.
I do not know, so we will see.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Remind your child about the safety rule: never point the lens at the Sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lens test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Close the curtains of the other windows to dim the room. Leave one window that does not show the Sun, or use a lamp across the room. Stand the card upright against a book. Hold the lens between the window and the card.
flow.say: Dim the room. Stand the card up. Hold the lens between the bright window and the card, near the card. Do not point the lens at the Sun.
flow.kid: Dim the room. Stand the card up. Hold the lens between the window and the card.
flow.parent: The window must be bright, but must not show the Sun. A window facing away from the Sun is best. Or use a bright lamp across the room. Never point the lens at the Sun, because it can burn.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the room, the card and the lens.

flow.do: Hold the lens and move it slowly towards and away from the card. Stop when a small, sharp picture of the window appears. Measure the distance from the lens to the card. Write it in the table. Write which way up the picture is.
flow.say: Move the lens slowly, closer to the card and then away. Stop when a sharp picture of the window appears. How far is the lens from the card? Which way up is the picture?
flow.kid: Move the lens slowly. Find a sharp picture of the window. Measure how far the card is.
flow.parent: You should see a small, coloured, upside-down picture of the window, with the frame and maybe a tree. It is small and a little dim. Dim the room more if it is faint. The sharp place is a narrow range, so move slowly. For a small magnifying glass, the card is typically about 10 to 20 centimetres from the lens. The lens of reading glasses is weaker, so the card may be 30 to 60 centimetres away, and the picture is bigger. If you see only a bright blur, the card is not at the sharp place yet. If nothing shows, make the room darker, and check that the lens is the kind that is thicker in the middle. Roles for 2 to 4 children: one holds the lens, one holds the card, one measures, one writes. Swap, so everyone finds the sharp picture once. One child alone with a parent: the child holds the lens, and the parent holds the card and measures.

check.q: The picture of the window on the card was upside down. Why?
options: The lens bends the rays from the top of the window downwards and from the bottom upwards, so the rays cross
The window was upside down
The card was held upside down
check.why: Rays from the top of the window go in a straight line down through the lens. Rays from the bottom go up. They cross at the lens, so the top of the window ends up at the bottom of the picture. Picking 'the window was upside down' is a fair first thought. But the same window looks the right way up to your eye.

flow.context: In this step, you find the sharp picture of a far window and measure how far the card is from the lens.

flow.do: Stand the phone, with a big black letter F on a bright white screen, about 50 centimetres from the lens. Move the card until a sharp picture of the F appears. Measure again from the lens to the card. Write whether the card is nearer or further than before.
flow.say: Now a bright thing that is nearer. The phone screen with a big F, half a metre away. Find the sharp picture on the card. Is the card nearer or further than for the window? Is the F upside down?
flow.kid: Use the phone with a big F, half a metre away. Find the sharp picture. Is the card nearer or further now?
flow.parent: For a small magnifying glass, the card typically has to move about 2 to 6 centimetres further from the lens than for the window. Measure carefully and write what you really see. If the card does not seem to need moving, try the phone nearer, at about 30 centimetres. The F should be small and upside down, and the picture is dimmer than the screen. Turn the screen brightness to the top and keep the room dim.

check.q: The bright phone screen was nearer to the lens. The card had to be a little further from the lens for a sharp picture. What does this show?
options: A lens needs the card in a different place for near things and far things
The lens got bigger
The phone was brighter than the window
check.why: A lens brings the rays from a near thing together a little further behind it than the rays from a far thing. So the card has to move. Picking 'the lens got bigger' is not right, because the same lens was used. In your eye, the retina cannot move, so the eye changes the lens instead.

chart.title: Made-up example: how a filled-in table can look
rows: The phone screen with an F

flow.context: In this step, you find the sharp picture of a nearer bright thing, and compare the card's place.

flow.do: Ask your child: your retina cannot move back and forth like the card. What must change in your eye when you look from a far window to a near book?
flow.say: The card had to move for near and far things. Your retina cannot move. So what must change in your eye when you look from a far window to a near book?
flow.kid: The card moved. Your retina cannot. What changes in your eye?
flow.parent: A good answer: the lens in the eye changes shape. It gets thicker for near things, which bends the rays more, and thinner for far things. This is called focusing.
flow.think: The lens in your eye can change shape. Which shape do you think it takes for a near book?
flow.context: In this step, you link the lens test to how the eye focuses.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about lenses? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a lens makes an upside-down picture of a bright thing. What I saw: a small upside-down window on the card, and the card had to move for a nearer thing. Why: the lens bends the rays from each point of the thing so that they meet again on the card.
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

activities.title: Hole in Your Hand: two eyes, two pictures

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, to roll into a tube about 3 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long
tape to hold the tube
a plain wall or a window to look at across the room
a pencil and a notebook

schedule.what: Make a tube. See a hole in your hand. Find out which eye leads.

activities.record: Draw your hand with the hole in it. Write which eye you found to be your leading eye, and which eyes your family members favour.
activities.context: In this activity, you look through a paper tube with one eye and at your hand with the other. You see a hole in your hand, and learn how the brain joins two pictures.

setup.art: A child rolling a sheet of paper into a tube and taping it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll a paper tube about 3 centimetres wide.

setup.art: A child holding the tube to her right eye with one hand and her left hand flat against the side of the tube, both eyes open.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the tube to one eye. Put the other hand beside the tube. Keep both eyes open.

setup.art: The child seeing a round hole in her left palm with the far wall visible through it.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the hole in your hand.

flow.do: Roll the paper into a tube about 3 centimetres wide and tape it. Ask your child to guess what they will see. They look through the tube with one eye, and at their hand with the other.
flow.say: Here is a paper tube. Look through it with one eye. Keep the other eye on your hand beside it. What do you think you will see?
flow.kid: Look through the tube with one eye. Keep the other eye on your hand. What will you see?

ask.q: What do you think you will see on your hand?
good: Nothing special.
A round spot.
A hole.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess is fine. It is a surprise for most children.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hole in Your Hand. You make the tube, and you guess before you test.

flow.do: Hold the tube to the right eye with the right hand. Hold the left hand open, palm towards you. Put it flat against the side of the tube, about 10 centimetres from the face. Keep both eyes open. Look at a far wall. Slide the hand until you see a hole in your palm.
flow.say: Tube to your right eye. Left hand beside the tube. Both eyes open. Look at the far wall. Do you see a hole in your hand?
flow.kid: Tube to one eye. Hand beside the tube. Both eyes open. Do you see a hole?
flow.parent: It works for most people in a few tries. If it does not, move the hand a little closer to the tube, and try the other eye. Some people need to adjust the tube a few times. The hole is a real result of two pictures being joined. Typically it works within a few tries. If it does not, make the tube a little wider or narrower, and keep the hand flat against the tube. Every child makes their own tube. Siblings can work in pairs: one tries, the other watches and adjusts the hand. Ask each child to draw what they see.

check.q: You see a round hole in your hand, but your hand is solid. Why does it seem to have a hole?
options: The brain joins the picture from each eye, so the round view through the tube seems to sit in the hand
The tube makes a hole in the hand
The hand is thin
check.why: One eye sees the circle of the far wall through the tube. The other eye sees the palm. The brain lays one picture on the other, so the circle of wall seems to be inside the hand. Picking 'the tube makes a hole' cannot be right, because your hand is still whole when you look at it with both eyes.

flow.context: In this step, you look through the tube and see the hole in your hand.

flow.do: Find your leading eye. Make a triangle with both hands at arm's length. Look through it at a far light switch with both eyes. Close the left eye, then the right. The eye that keeps the switch in the triangle is the leading eye.
flow.say: Make a small triangle with your hands, at arm's length. Look at a far light switch through it. Close one eye, then the other. Which eye keeps the switch in the hole?
flow.kid: Make a triangle with your hands. Look at a far switch. Close one eye, then the other. Which keeps it?
flow.parent: Most people favour the right eye, but many favour the left. The leading eye is the one the brain uses when the two pictures disagree. It does not mean that the other eye is weaker.
flow.think: Most people favour one eye, as they favour one hand. What do you notice about who in your family favours the left eye?
flow.context: In this step, you find which of your eyes leads.

activities.title: How Wide Can You See? The clock-face test

materials.item: 12 sheets of paper, numbered 1 to 12 like a clock, or chalk to draw a clock face on the floor
a chair for the person being tested
a string 1 metre long, to lay out the circle
a bright red pen, or a red object on a stick (a bigger red object, such as a red card 5 centimetres across, is easier to see at the edge)
a sticker or a mark on the wall in front, at eye height, to stare at
a helper to move the pen round the circle
a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: Lay out a clock face on the floor. Move a red pen in from behind, and find where you notice movement and where you can name its colour.

activities.record: Fill in the table. Draw a top-down picture of a head with two wedges showing how wide you could see movement, and how wide you could name the colour.
activities.context: In this activity, you sit in the middle of a clock face on the floor and stare straight ahead. A helper moves a red pen in from behind. You find where you notice it and where you can name its colour.

setup.art: Twelve numbered papers in a circle on the floor, 1 metre from a chair at the centre, with a sticker on the wall at 12 o'clock.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the clock face. Put the chair in the middle.

setup.art: A child on the chair staring at the sticker, with a helper walking a red pen along the circle from the 6 o'clock paper.
setup.caption: 2. Stare at the sticker. The helper moves the pen in from behind.

setup.art: The child saying 'now' as the pen reaches the 3 o'clock paper, and the helper writing it in the table.
setup.caption: 3. Say 'now' when you notice the pen move. Say 'red' when you can name its colour.

flow.do: Show your child the clock face on the floor. Ask them to guess where on the clock they will first notice the pen moving. Ask where they will first be able to name its colour.
flow.say: You will sit in the middle and stare straight ahead at the sticker. I will move a red pen in from behind you. Where on the clock will you first notice it? Where will you first know that it is red?
flow.kid: Stare at the sticker. A pen comes in from behind. Where will you notice it? Where will you know it is red?

ask.q: Will you notice the pen moving before you can say its colour, or after?
good: Before, because movement is easy to see.
After, because I need to see it to know it moves.
At the same time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the clock-face test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Lay the 12 papers in a circle around the chair, 1 metre from it, like a clock. Put 12 straight ahead and 6 behind. Put a sticker on the wall at 12 o'clock at eye height. Your child sits on the chair.
flow.say: Lay out the clock on the floor. Twelve is straight ahead and six is behind. Sit in the middle and look at the sticker on the wall. Do not move your eyes.
flow.kid: Lay the papers in a circle. Sit in the middle. Stare at the sticker. Do not move your eyes.
flow.parent: Each paper is 30 degrees from the next, because a full circle is 360 degrees and there are 12 papers. Eleven o'clock is on the left and one o'clock is on the right.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the clock face and sit in the middle.

flow.do: Start behind the chair at the 6 paper on the right side. Move the red pen slowly along the circle towards 12, at arm's length from the circle. Your child says 'now' when they notice any movement. Write the hour paper. Keep going. They say 'red' when they can name the colour. Write that hour paper.
flow.say: Keep staring at the sticker. I will move the pen in from behind. Say 'now' when you notice it moving. Say 'red' when you are sure of its colour.
flow.kid: Stare at the sticker. Say 'now' when you notice movement. Say 'red' when you know its colour.
flow.parent: Make sure the eyes stay on the sticker. If you see them move, start again. Typically movement is noticed at about the 3 paper or a little behind it, and the red colour is named at about the 1 or 2 paper. People differ, so write what you really see. Do not tell your child the numbers until the end. Wiggle the pen a little as you walk, because a still pen at the edge may not be noticed. Walk quietly, and do not make a sound, so that sound does not give it away. Roles for 2 to 4 children: one sits, one walks the pen, one writes, one watches the sitter's eyes. Swap after each side. One child alone with a parent: the parent walks the pen and watches the eyes, and the child writes the result afterwards.

check.q: You noticed the pen moving much earlier than you could say it was red. Why?
options: The edges of the retina notice movement well, but have few cone cells for colour
Red is hard to see
The pen changed colour as it moved
check.why: The edges of your retina have many rod cells, which are good at noticing movement and dim light, but only a few cone cells, which see colour. So you notice movement first, and colour later, as the pen moves closer to your sharp spot. Picking 'the pen changed colour' sounds sensible, but the pen stayed red the whole time.

flow.context: In this step, you test the right side of your view and write down what you find.

flow.do: Repeat on the left side, from 6 towards 12. Write the two hour papers. Compare the left side with the right side, and then with another person if you can.
flow.say: Now the left side. Same rules. Say 'now' for movement, and 'red' for colour. Then we compare.
flow.kid: Now the left side. Say 'now' for movement. Say 'red' for colour.
flow.parent: Left and right usually give similar results. A person with glasses should wear them for the test. Draw the two wedges on a top-down picture of a head, one for movement and one for colour.
flow.think: You can see a lot without turning your head, but you only see colour well in a smaller space. What does that say about how much of the world you really see in colour at one time?
flow.context: In this step, you test the left side of your view and compare your results.

activities.title: Near Point: how close can you focus?

materials.item: a card with a line of small writing on it, with letters about 3 millimetres tall, written with a fine pen
a ruler or a measuring tape
at least two family members of different ages, such as a child, a parent and a grandparent
a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: Find the nearest distance at which you can still read the small writing. Test other people in the family and compare.

activities.record: Fill in the table with each person's age and near point. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each person.
activities.context: In this activity, you bring a card with small writing slowly towards your eye until it turns blurry. You measure the distance, which is your near point, and compare with people of other ages.

setup.art: A card with a line of small writing being held at arm's length by a child, with one eye covered.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the card at arm's length. Cover one eye.

setup.art: The same card brought slowly closer, with a ruler held by a helper measuring from the card to the child's eye.
setup.caption: 2. Bring the card closer until the writing turns blurry. Stop. Measure.

setup.art: A row of three people of different ages, with their near points marked on a ruler: short, medium and long.
setup.caption: 3. Test other people and compare.

flow.do: Show your child the card. Ask them to guess who in the family can read the card closest to their eyes. Ask who will need it furthest away. Write the guesses.
flow.say: We will bring a card with small writing closer to the eye until the words turn blurry. Who in our family do you think will manage the closest? Who the furthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Bring the writing close until it blurs. Who in our family can go closest? Why?

ask.q: Who do you think will have the closest near point, and why?
good: The child, because her eyes are young.
The grandparent, because she has seen so much.
Everyone is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Remember to ask the person to take off reading glasses for the test. Hold the card steady and keep its sharp corners away from the eye. If someone cannot read even at arm's length, write 'more than arm's length'. For 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one tests, one measures and writes, then swap. For one child, a parent measures.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Near Point test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Ask your child to cover the left eye with a hand and hold the card at arm's length. Read the small writing. Bring the card slowly closer, until the writing first turns blurry. Stop. Hold still. The helper measures from the card to the corner of the eye. Do it three times.
flow.say: Cover one eye. Hold the card at arm's length. Bring it slowly closer. Stop the moment the words turn blurry. I will measure.
flow.kid: Cover one eye. Bring the card slowly closer. Stop when the words blur. Someone measures.
flow.parent: The near point is the closest distance with sharp writing. Move the card slowly. Do not press the hand on the covered eye. Take the middle of the three numbers. Children's near points are often 7 to 12 centimetres.

check.q: The writing turned blurry when the card came too near. What does this tell you about the lens in the eye?
options: The lens cannot get thick enough to focus on things that close
The card changed
The eye ran out of light
check.why: To focus on a near thing, the lens must get thicker. It has a limit. Closer than that limit, the picture on the retina is blurry. Picking 'the eye ran out of light' is a natural idea. But the writing was still lit. The problem was the focus, not the light.

flow.context: In this step, you find and measure your own near point.

flow.do: Repeat the test with two other family members of different ages. Write their ages and near points in the table. Remind them to take off reading glasses.
flow.say: Now test someone older. And someone else. How close can they go? Is it the same as you?
flow.kid: Test two other people. Write their ages and near points.
flow.parent: Typical near points: a child, 7 to 12 centimetres. An adult in the forties, 15 to 30 centimetres. A person over 60, 40 to 100 centimetres or more. People vary a lot. If someone cannot read even at arm's length, they may need reading glasses and an eye test. That is normal with age.

chart.title: Made-up example: near point of three people

flow.context: In this step, you measure the near point of other people in your family and write down the ages.

flow.do: Look at the table or bar chart. Ask your child what pattern they see. Ask why the lens might be less able to get thick as people get older.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. Who had the closest near point? Who the furthest? What pattern do you see?
flow.kid: Look at the numbers. What pattern do you see?
flow.parent: A good answer: older people have a further near point, because the lens gets stiffer and cannot thicken as much. Reading glasses add a lens in front of the eye to help.
flow.think: The lens gets stiffer with age. How does that change the near point?
flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern and think about what it means.

activities.title: How Big Does It Look? A ruler at arm's length

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler
a friend or family member who can stand still for a minute, holding upright a pole exactly 60 centimetres tall (a stick, a rolled newspaper or a broom handle cut to size, measured with the ruler)

a corridor, a long room or a terrace at least 8 metres long, with marks at 2, 4 and 8 metres (use a tape measure and chalk or tape). If your space is shorter, use marks at 1, 2 and 4 metres and a 30 centimetre pole
a tape measure
a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: Measure how tall a 60 centimetre pole looks on a ruler at arm's length when it stands at 2, 4 and 8 metres. Find the pattern.

activities.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each distance. Write what happened to the apparent height each time the distance doubled.
activities.context: In this activity, you hold a ruler at arm's length and measure how tall a pole looks when a friend holds it at different distances. You find out how the size that a thing looks depends on its distance.

setup.art: A corridor with chalk marks at 2, 4 and 8 metres, a friend holding a pole upright at the 2 metre mark, and a child holding a ruler at arm's length.
setup.caption: 1. Mark 2, 4 and 8 metres. A friend holds the pole upright at the first mark.

setup.art: A child with one eye closed holding a ruler at arm's length, with the thumb lined up with the bottom of the pole and the top of the pole read on the ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the ruler at arm's length. Read how tall the pole looks.

setup.art: The same view with the pole at 4 metres, seeming half as tall on the ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Repeat at 4 and 8 metres.

flow.do: Show your child the ruler, the pole and the marks. Ask: the pole moves from 2 metres to 4 metres. How tall will it look on the ruler? The same? Half? Why do you think so?
flow.say: We will measure how tall a pole looks on a ruler at arm's length. At 2 metres, then 4 metres, then 8. What happens to its height on the ruler when it moves back? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Measure a pole on a ruler. It moves back. What happens to its height on the ruler? Why?

ask.q: What will happen to its height on the ruler when it is twice as far away?
good: It will be half as big.
It will stay the same, because she is the same size.
It will get a bit smaller.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Big Does It Look. You guess before you test.

flow.do: The friend stands at the 2 metre mark, holding the pole upright with its bottom on the floor. Your child holds the ruler upright at arm's length, with the elbow locked. They close one eye. Line up the 0 mark with the bottom of the pole. Read the number, in centimetres and millimetres, at the top of the pole. Write it down. Do it twice.
flow.say: Hold the ruler out at arm's length with a straight arm. Close one eye. Line up the 0 with the bottom of the pole. What number is at the top of the pole?
flow.kid: Hold the ruler at arm's length. Close one eye. Read how tall the pole looks.
flow.parent: Keep the arm straight and the ruler the same distance from the eye each time. Use the same eye each time. A 60 centimetre pole at 2 metres typically looks about 12 to 18 centimetres tall on the ruler, so the ruler is long enough. The friend must hold the pole upright and still, with its bottom on the mark. Ask the friend to stand next to the pole and not behind it, so that the reader can see the pole clearly. Do the test in a safe place, away from traffic and stairs. For 2 to 4 children: one reads the ruler, one holds the pole, one writes. Swap, and compare the readings of different children, who have different arm lengths. For one child with a parent: the parent holds the pole and writes.
flow.context: In this step, you measure how tall the pole looks at 2 metres.

flow.do: The friend moves to the 4 metre mark, and then to the 8 metre mark, with the pole. Measure how tall the pole looks on the ruler at each, using the same arm, the same eye and the same ruler.
flow.say: Now the pole moves back to four metres. How tall does it look on the ruler now? And at eight?
flow.kid: The pole moves back. Measure again at 4 metres and at 8 metres.
flow.parent: Typically the apparent height halves, roughly, each time the distance doubles. If the pole is 60 centimetres tall and your arm's length is about 50 centimetres, it should look about 15 centimetres tall at 2 metres, about 7 to 8 at 4 metres and about 4 at 8 metres. Your numbers will differ. Measurements are rough, because it is hard to read a ruler at arm's length. At 8 metres, read to the nearest millimetre, and do it twice.

check.q: The pole looked half as tall at 4 metres as at 2 metres. What does this show about distance and size?
options: Twice as far away makes a thing look half as tall
A thing gets smaller when it moves
The ruler shrank
check.why: The rays from the top and bottom of the pole make an angle at your eye. Twice as far means half the angle, so it looks half as tall. The pole did not shrink, and neither did the ruler. Picking 'a thing gets smaller' mixes up how it looks with how big it is.

chart.title: Made-up example: how tall a 60 cm pole looked on the ruler
cols: How tall it looked on the ruler

flow.context: In this step, you measure at 4 metres and 8 metres.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart of your three measurements. Ask what happens to the height each time the distance doubles.
flow.say: Look at your three numbers. What happens each time she steps twice as far away?
flow.kid: Look at your three numbers. What pattern do you see?
flow.think: If you wanted a sign to look the same size from twice as far away, how big would you have to make it?
flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern in the numbers.

projects.title: A Bird in a Cage: pictures that join in your eye

materials.item: stiff card from an old cereal box, for two discs about 8 centimetres across
a pencil and a mug or glass to draw round
felt pens or colour pencils
glue or tape, and scissors for a grown-up to use
two pieces of string or wool, each about 30 centimetres long, or one long rubber band
a small notepad of at least 15 pages, or 15 sticky notes stuck in a pile
a pen for the flip book

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts out the card discs with scissors.

schedule.what: Make the thaumatrope. Make the flip book. Test them at different speeds.

projects.record: Keep the thaumatrope and the flip book. Draw the bird and the cage joined together, as you saw them. Write how fast you had to twirl or flick for the pictures to join.
projects.context: In this project, you make a card with a bird on one side and a cage on the other, and a flip book. You find out how pictures that come quickly join in your eye and brain.

setup.art: A round card disc with a bird drawn on the front, and the same disc turned over with a cage drawn on the back.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a bird on one side of a disc and a cage on the other.

setup.art: The disc with a string on each side, being twirled between two thumbs and fingers, and a bird seen inside the cage.
setup.caption: 2. Twirl the disc on its strings. The bird seems to be inside the cage.

setup.art: A small notepad with a ball drawn on the corner of each page in slightly different places, being flicked by a thumb.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a flip book and flick the pages.

flow.do: Show your child the card, the strings and the notepad. Ask what they think will happen if a bird on one side and a cage on the other are twirled very quickly.
flow.say: We will draw a bird on one side of a card and a cage on the other. Then we twirl it very fast. What do you think we will see? Why?
flow.kid: A bird on one side. A cage on the other. We twirl the card. What will you see? Why?

ask.q: What will you see when the card spins fast?
good: Just a blur.
The bird inside the cage.
A bird, then a cage, then a bird.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Bird in a Cage. You guess before you make.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts two discs from the card by drawing round a mug. Draw a bird on one disc. Flip the disc over like a page, top to bottom, and note which way up the back is. On the second disc, draw a cage, the right way up when it is flipped in the same way. Glue the two discs back to back with a string between them on each side.
flow.say: Draw a bird on one disc. Draw a cage on the other. Make the cage the right way up when you flip the card like a page. Glue the two discs together with a string on each side.
flow.kid: Draw a bird on one disc and a cage on the other. Glue them back to back with strings.
flow.parent: The two pictures must be the right way up for each other when the card is flipped by twirling it between the strings. A good way: draw the bird, then flip the card over like a page of a calendar, and draw the cage on the back so that it looks right way up in that position. Make both pictures simple and bold, in the middle of the disc. If the bird and cage do not line up, redraw.

check.q: Why do the two pictures have to be drawn in the middle of each disc?
options: So that they sit on top of each other when the disc flips quickly
So that the disc is easy to cut
Because bright colours show best there
check.why: When the disc twirls, each picture lands in the same place as the other one. The brain joins them there. If one picture were off to the side, the two would not overlap, and you would just see two flickering pictures. Picking 'easy to cut' is about looks, not about what you see.

flow.context: In this step, you make the thaumatrope.

flow.do: Hold the two strings between your thumbs and first fingers. Twirl the strings so that the disc spins fast. Look at the disc as it spins. Say what you see. Try spinning it slowly and then quickly.
flow.say: Hold the strings and twirl the disc. Look at it as it spins. What do you see now? What happens when it spins slowly?
flow.kid: Twirl the disc. What do you see? Spin it slowly, too. What changes?
flow.parent: At a fast spin, the bird should seem to sit inside the cage. At a slow spin, you see the bird, then the cage, flicking. If the picture does not join, spin faster, or redraw the pictures bolder and in the middle. To spin fast: twist the strings by rolling them between the fingers about 20 times, then pull the strings gently apart and let the disc untwist. Typically the join is clear at about 10 spins a second, so the strings must be tight. Each child makes their own disc, with their own pictures (for example a fish and a bowl, or a flower and a vase). Swap discs and guess what the other child drew on the hidden side. One child alone with a parent: make two discs and compare.
flow.context: In this step, you twirl the thaumatrope and look at what happens.

flow.do: Use the notepad. On the corner of the last page, draw a small ball at the bottom. On the page before it, draw the ball a little higher. Go on, page by page, moving the ball up and then down. Flick the pages from the first to the last with your thumb.
flow.say: Draw a little ball at the corner of each page, a bit higher each time. Then flick the pages with your thumb. What do you see?
flow.kid: Draw a ball on each page. Move it a bit each time. Flick the pages. What do you see?
flow.parent: Draw from the back of the pad to the front, so the flick runs from the first page to the last. Keep the ball the same size and move it a small amount each time. About 15 pages is enough to make a short bounce, but 25 or more pages last longer. Press hard with a pen so that the ball shows, and draw it near the corner where the thumb flicks the pages. If the pages are thick, the ball may be hard to see through the page, so use a dark pen. The smaller the moves, the smoother the motion. Scientists have long said that the eye holds on to each picture for a moment, called persistence of vision. Many now think that the brain also builds movement from still pictures. They are still working out how.

check.q: In your flip book, each page is a still picture. Why does the ball seem to move?
options: The brain joins the pictures that come quickly one after another, and sees movement
The ball is moving on the page
The pages are warm
check.why: Each page is still. But when they come quickly one after another, your brain joins them and builds movement between them. Films work the same way. Picking 'the ball is moving on the page' can be tested. Stop flicking and look at one page: the ball is still.

flow.context: In this step, you make a flip book of a bouncing ball.

flow.do: Flick the flip book slowly, one page a second. Then at a medium speed. Then fast. Time each flick with a phone stopwatch. Work out pages each second: pages divided by seconds. Write down the speed at which the ball moves smoothly. Write the speed at which it looks like separate pictures. It typically looks smooth at about 10 pages a second or more. A short pad takes only about 1 second, so flick it several times.
flow.say: Flick the flip book slowly. What do you see? Now medium. Now fast. When does the ball seem to move smoothly?
flow.kid: Flick slowly. Flick medium. Flick fast. When does the ball seem to move?
flow.think: A film shows 24 still pictures every second. Why do you think it seems smooth?
flow.context: In this step, you test different speeds of your flip book.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about how we see pictures that come quickly? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: pictures that come quickly join in my eye and brain. What I saw: the bird was inside the cage when the disc spun fast, and the ball seemed to move in the flip book. Why: the brain joins pictures that come close together in time.
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

challenges.title: Readable From the Far End: design the best sign
challenges.problem: A visitor is looking for your door from the far end of the lane or corridor. Make a sign with one word on it that a friend can read from as far away as possible. Find out which size of letter and which pair of colours can be read from the furthest distance.
constraints: Use one sheet of paper or chart paper for each sign, and one plain word in capital letters, such as EXIT or HOME.
Test every sign in the same light, with the same reader, and let her wear her glasses if she has them.
Measure the distance at which the reader can first read every letter, with a tape measure or with big steps that you have measured once.
Change only one thing between two signs, so that you know what made the difference.
materials: chart paper or A4 sheets, plain white and yellow if possible
thick felt pens in black, red, green, blue and yellow
a ruler, to draw straight letters
a corridor, a terrace or a lane at least 10 metres long
a tape measure or a string with knots every metre
a friend or family member to be the reader
general: Make the letters bigger. A thing twice as tall can be read from about twice as far.
Use thick strokes, so each letter makes a bold shape.
Use two colours that are very different in brightness, such as black on white or black on yellow.
creative: Leave a wide gap between letters, so that they do not run together from far away.
Add a thick black border round the word, so the eye finds it first.
Try colours that are alike in brightness, such as red on green, and see why signs do not use them. Remember that some people see red and green alike.
challenges.your_turn: Now design the best sign for your own front door. Draw it, make it and test it from the lane. How far away could your friend read it? How could you make it readable from further?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about seeing. You make signs and find out how big and what colour the letters must be to be read from far away.

setup.art: Four paper signs with the word EXIT in different sizes and colours laid on a table beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Make signs with different letter sizes and colours.

setup.art: A child standing at the far end of a corridor with a friend walking towards her holding a sign, and a measuring tape on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. The reader stands still. The sign-holder walks towards her.

flow.do: Read the challenge together. Ask your child what they think makes a sign easy to read from far away.
flow.say: Here is your job. Make a sign that a friend can read from as far away as possible. What do you think makes a sign easy to read from far away?
flow.kid: Make a sign that is easy to read from far. What helps? Big letters? Colours?

ask.q: What do you think will make a sign easier to read from far away?
good: Bigger letters.
Thicker letters.
A bright colour against a dark one.

flow.parent: Let your child make a plan. A good plan changes one thing at a time. Do not give the answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Readable From the Far End challenge. You read the problem and make a plan.

flow.do: Make the first sign: the word EXIT in black letters 1 centimetre tall on white paper. The reader stands at the far end. The sign-holder walks towards her. When the reader can read every letter, she says 'now'. Measure the distance and write it down.
flow.say: Make a sign with one word in black, with small letters one centimetre tall. Hold it up and walk towards your reader. She says 'now' when she can read every letter. How far is that?
flow.kid: Make a sign with small black letters. Walk towards the reader. She says 'now' when she can read it.
flow.parent: A letter 1 centimetre tall can typically be read from about 4 to 7 metres. Make sure the reader does not know the word in advance, or she will guess. Change the word each time. The reader's eyes and the light matter, so keep them the same.

chart.title: Made-up example: how a filled-in table can look

flow.context: In this step, you make the first sign and find how far away it can be read.

flow.do: Make more signs, changing one thing each time. Try letters 2 centimetres tall in black on white. Then go back to letters 1 centimetre tall. Try black on yellow, yellow on white, and red on green, all 1 centimetre tall. Test each one the same way. Write each distance.
flow.say: Now change one thing at a time. First make the letters twice as tall. Then try different colours. Which sign can be read from furthest? Which from the closest?
flow.kid: Change one thing at a time. Bigger letters. Different colours. Test each sign. Write each distance.
flow.parent: Letters twice as tall are usually readable from about twice as far. Black on white or black on yellow usually beat yellow on white and red on green, because they differ more in brightness. Compare colours with the 1 centimetre letters, so that every sign can be read within your space. If the reader can read a sign from the whole length of your space, make the letters smaller, 5 millimetres, and test again. For 2 to 4 children: take turns as reader, sign-holder and recorder, and have each child design one sign. Test in a safe place, away from traffic. Write what you really see. Some people see red and green as nearly the same, so signs rarely use that pair.

check.q: A word with letters 2 centimetres tall could be read from twice as far as the same word with letters 1 centimetre tall. Why?
options: Twice as tall at twice the distance makes the same angle at the eye, so it looks the same size
Bigger letters are brighter
The reader's eyes got better
check.why: The size that a thing looks depends on the angle between the rays from its top and its bottom. Doubling the height and the distance together keeps the angle the same. Picking 'brighter' is not right, because the paper and the pen were the same. Picking 'eyes got better' fails, because the reader and her eyes did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you test signs with different sizes and colours and write down how far each can be read.

flow.do: Look at all your distances. Ask your child which sign won, and why. Ask which change mattered most.
flow.say: Look at your table. Which sign could be read from furthest? Which change mattered most, the size or the colour? Why?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which sign won? What mattered most?
flow.think: Road signs for fast drivers have very big letters. How much bigger must they be than a sign in a corridor, to be read in time?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the signs and explain what you found.

quiz.p: What is the best evidence that light travels in straight lines?
opts: The spot of light vanishes when one of three cards with holes is slid sideways
Light is very bright
Light travels fast
quiz.why: The spot only reached the wall when the holes were on one straight line. Brightness and speed do not say anything about the path.

quiz.p: In a ray diagram, what do the arrows show?
opts: The direction that the light travels
How hot the light is
Where the eye is looking
quiz.why: A ray is a straight arrow that shows where a thin beam of light is going. In the diagram of a lamp, a mango and an eye, every arrow points the way the light travels.

quiz.p: A magnifying glass held between a window and a card makes a picture on the card. How does the picture look?
opts: Small and upside down
Big and the right way up
Just a blur of light
quiz.why: A lens makes an upside-down picture of a far window on a card, if the card is at the sharp place. It is small, because the window is far away.

quiz.p: You look from a book to a far tree. What does the lens in your eye do?
opts: It gets thinner
It gets thicker
It moves back
quiz.why: A thick lens bends light a lot, for near things. A thinner lens bends light less, for far things.

quiz.p: You swap eyes with a finger held up, and the finger jumps. Where does the finger give the biggest jump?
opts: Close to your nose
At arm's length
Across the room
quiz.why: The nearer the finger, the bigger the jump. The brain uses this to tell how far away things are.

quiz.p: An owl hunts at night. Where are her eyes, and why?
opts: At the front, so that two overlapping views give depth for a pounce
At the sides, so that she can see all round
On top of her head, so that she can see up
quiz.why: A hunter needs depth to judge a leap. Front eyes overlap, and the difference between the views gives depth.

quiz.p: Which sentence is the best reasoning for 'touching the tips of two pencils is harder with one eye'?
opts: With one eye, the brain loses the difference between two views that tells it how far away the tips are
One eye is weaker than two
Pencils are hard to see
quiz.why: Reasoning says why. It uses what we know about two views and depth. 'One eye is weaker' does not explain anything.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists not agree on yet?
opts: Exactly why the Moon looks bigger near the horizon
That light travels in straight lines in clear air
That two eyes give two different pictures
quiz.why: The other two have been tested many times. The reason for the Moon illusion is still argued about.

quiz.p: A friend stands 8 metres away and looks half as tall as she looks at 4 metres. Why?
opts: The rays from her head and feet make a smaller angle at your eye
She shrinks when she walks away
Light travels slower far away
quiz.why: Twice as far means half the angle at the eye, so she looks half as tall. She did not shrink.

quiz.p: What best explains the blind spot?
opts: The optic nerve leaves the eye there, so there are no light-catching cells
The lens is thin there
The pupil blocks the light
quiz.why: The nerve fibres gather and leave the eye at one place, and there are no light-catching cells in that place.

quiz.p: Why can a person with one eye still judge distance quite well?
opts: They use clues such as size, overlap and how things shift when the head moves
Their one eye is twice as strong
They cannot, but they guess well
quiz.why: There are many clues to distance in one view. Moving the head gives two views, one after the other, just as two eyes give two at once.

quiz.p: A sign must be read from twice as far away. How tall should its letters be?
opts: About twice as tall
About half as tall
The same height
quiz.why: Twice as far makes the angle half as big. Twice as tall makes it twice as big again, so the sign looks the same size.

applications: Eye doctors test how well each eye focuses, and prescribe glasses with convex or concave lenses.
Eye camps and eye hospitals across India test eyes and give out glasses.
Cameras and phone cameras use a lens to focus a sharp picture on a sensor, as the eye focuses on the retina.
3D films and virtual reality headsets show a slightly different picture to each eye, so that the brain builds depth.
Robot cars and drones use two cameras to measure distance by the same method as two eyes.
Astronomers measure the distance to some nearby stars by looking from two places half a year apart.
Road and railway signs use big letters and high-contrast colours, so they can be read in time from far away.
Binoculars give each eye its own tube and its own view.
Cricketers and other ball players train to predict where a ball will land.
Films and animation show still pictures one after another, 24 or more each second, and the brain sees movement.
Reflective strips and bright jackets help drivers to notice walkers at dusk, because the edges of the eye are good at spotting movement and brightness.
Painters use size, overlap and haze to give a flat picture the look of depth.
Pinhole cameras and the camera obscura were used by painters and scientists to make pictures of scenes.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn two flat pictures into one solid world?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many steps and many parts of the brain that work on depth. But nobody knows how those steps become the experience of seeing a solid world.

open_questions.q: Why does the Moon look bigger near the horizon?
open_questions.why_open: People have argued about this for more than a thousand years. Several effects probably work together, but no single idea explains all the tests.

open_questions.q: Why is short sight getting more common in children, and does time outdoors really help?
open_questions.why_open: Studies in several countries suggest that more time outdoors in daylight lowers the chance of short sight. Scientists are still working out why, and what else matters.

open_questions.q: Can a person who never had two-eyed depth vision learn it later?
open_questions.why_open: Susan Barry, a neuroscientist in the USA, gained depth vision as an adult and wrote about it. Scientists used to think this was impossible. They are now studying how often it can happen.

open_questions.q: How does the brain decide which parts of the left eye's picture go with which parts of the right eye's picture?
open_questions.why_open: The two pictures are full of similar-looking bits. The brain matches them very quickly, but exactly how it avoids mistakes is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How does the brain predict where a fast ball will be?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure how fielders move and what the brain does. They are still working out what rules the brain uses to make its prediction.

open_questions.q: What is it like to see with the eyes of an octopus or a hawk?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what their eyes respond to and what they can tell apart. We cannot get inside their experience, and we cannot ask them.

maths.problem: A child measured the jump of a pencil at three distances: 15 centimetres at 50 centimetres, 35 centimetres at 25 centimetres, and 80 centimetres at 15 centimetres. When the pencil moved from 50 to 25 centimetres, the distance halved. Did the jump less than double, exactly double or more than double?
maths.explain: The jump at 50 centimetres was 15 centimetres. Double that is 30. The jump at 25 centimetres was 35, which is more than 30. So the jump grew by more than double when the distance halved.
maths.context: In this experiment, you swap eyes while holding a pencil at different distances, and measure how far the pencil seems to jump against a strip on the wall.

chart.title: Made-up example: the jump at three distances
cols: Pencil held this far from the eyes

maths.why_maths: Comparing the jumps shows that the jump grows faster than the distance shrinks. That is why close things give the brain such a strong clue.

maths.problem: A pole looked 16 centimetres tall on a ruler at arm's length when it stood 2 metres away. How tall would it look at 4 metres? At 8 metres? At what distance would it look 2 centimetres tall?
maths.answer: 8 centimetres at 4 metres, 4 centimetres at 8 metres, and 2 centimetres at 16 metres.
maths.explain: Twice as far makes it look half as tall. Half of 16 is 8. Half of 8 is 4. Half of 4 is 2. That was three halvings, from 2 metres: 4, 8, then 16 metres.
maths.context: In this activity, you hold a ruler at arm's length and measure how tall a pole looks when a friend holds it at different distances.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again shows the pattern, and lets you work out a distance from a size you have measured.

maths.problem: The chart shows the near points of three people. How many times further is the grandparent's near point than the child's? How many centimetres further is it than the parent's?
maths.answer: 6 times further than the child's, and 24 centimetres further than the parent's.
maths.explain: The grandparent's near point is 48 centimetres and the child's is 8. 8 times 6 is 48, so it is 6 times further. The parent's is 24. 48 take away 24 is 24 centimetres.
maths.context: In this activity, you measure the nearest distance at which people of different ages can still read small writing.

chart.title: Made-up example: near point of three people

maths.why_maths: Comparing by multiplying and by subtracting shows how much the lens has stiffened with age, in two different ways.

maths.problem: In the Three Cards test, the middle card was slid sideways in steps. The spot was bright at 0 and 2 millimetres, dim at 4 millimetres and gone at 6, 8 and 10 millimetres. The holes were 5 millimetres wide. At which shift did the spot first dim? Is that close to the width of the hole? What does that suggest?
maths.answer: It first dimmed at 4 millimetres, which is close to the 5 millimetre width of the hole. It suggests that the light stops when the card moves about as far as the width of the hole.
maths.explain: The spot was bright up to 2 millimetres and dim at 4. The hole is 5 millimetres wide. 4 is a little less than 5. If the card moves about one hole-width, the holes no longer overlap, so the light cannot go straight through all three.
maths.context: In this experiment, you slide the middle card of three sideways in small steps and watch the spot of light on the wall.

chart.title: Made-up example: how the spot changed
cols: Spot of light on the wall

maths.why_maths: Comparing the shift with the width of the hole explains the result, and lets you predict what a bigger hole would do.

maths.problem: A clock face is a full circle of 360 degrees, and it has 12 hour marks. How many degrees are there between one hour mark and the next? In the clock-face test, a child noticed movement at the 3 mark and named the colour at the 1 mark, counted from the 12 straight ahead. How many degrees further out was the movement mark?
maths.answer: 30 degrees between hour marks. The movement mark was 60 degrees further out.
maths.explain: 360 divided by 12 is 30. So each hour mark is 30 degrees from the next. The 3 mark is 3 steps from the 12, so it is 90 degrees. The 1 mark is 1 step, so 30 degrees. 90 take away 30 is 60 degrees.
maths.context: In this activity, you sit in the middle of a clock face laid out on the floor and find where you can notice a moving pen and where you can name its colour.
maths.why_maths: Measuring angles in degrees turns 'a bit to the side' into a number that you can compare with other people's.

maths.problem: A tennis ball flies at 10 metres every second. The signals from the eye take about a tenth of a second to be used. How far does the ball move in a tenth of a second? What does that tell a fielder?
maths.answer: 1 metre. A fielder's brain is working with a picture in which the ball is already 1 metre behind its true place, so she must predict where the ball will be.
maths.explain: A tenth of a second is one tenth of one second. One tenth of 10 metres is 1 metre. So the ball has moved 1 metre by the time the picture is used. The fielder has to guess ahead.
maths.context: In this unit, you learn that what the brain uses to see is a little old, so a fielder has to predict where a ball will be.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by 10 shows how big the delay really is for a fast ball, and why prediction is needed.

maths.problem: Letters 1 centimetre tall could be read from 5 metres in the Readable From the Far End challenge. How far could letters 3 centimetres tall be read? How tall must letters be to be read from 40 metres?
maths.answer: 15 metres for 3 centimetre letters, and 8 centimetre letters for 40 metres.
maths.explain: Letters three times as tall can be read from three times as far, so 3 times 5 is 15 metres. For 40 metres, divide by 5. 40 divided by 5 is 8, so the letters must be 8 times as tall, which is 8 centimetres.
maths.context: In this challenge, you make signs with letters of different sizes and find how far away a friend can read them.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that size and distance go up together lets a designer work out how big a sign must be before making it.

maths.problem: Five children each tried five times to touch pencil tips together. With both eyes, they touched 4, 5, 4, 5 and 3 times. With one eye, they touched 2, 1, 3, 1 and 2 times. How many more touches were there with both eyes? What fraction of all the one-eye tries touched?
maths.answer: 12 more touches with both eyes. 9 out of 25 one-eye tries touched.
maths.explain: Both eyes: 4 plus 5 plus 4 plus 5 plus 3 is 21. One eye: 2 plus 1 plus 3 plus 1 plus 2 is 9. 21 take away 9 is 12. There were 5 times 5, which is 25 tries, so 9 out of 25 touched.
maths.context: In this experiment, you try to touch two pencil tips together with two eyes open, and then with one eye closed.

chart.title: Made-up example: touches out of 25 tries

maths.why_maths: Adding all the tries makes the pattern clear, and a fraction says how much worse one eye did.

roots.context: We have followed light in straight lines, made pictures with a hole and a lens, and used two views to find depth. Now we ask what this tells us about seeing and about the world it shows us.

deep_truth.truth: Hold up a finger and swap eyes, and it jumps against the wall. The jump is bigger for near things and smaller for far things. Your brain uses that difference to say how far away things are. So distance is worked out, not seen.
deep_truth.habit: We say we see how far away things are, as if distance were printed on them like a label. But nothing in a single view says how far away something is. The brain has to work it out from two views, or from clues such as size and overlap.
deep_truth.evidence: In the finger jump test, the pencil seemed to jump further when it was held near than when it was held far. When one eye was covered, touching two pencil tips together got harder. If your results are not clear, write them down honestly and try again with a longer strip on the wall.

three.who_am_i: You never look out from just one place. Your two eyes are about 6 centimetres apart, and your picture of the world is built from both of them.
three.what_is_life: Owls and tigers have both eyes at the front, to judge distance for a pounce. Deer and hens have eyes at the sides, to see almost all the way round. Each body is built for the life it leads.
three.what_is_this_world: A single view cannot show how far away things are. It takes two viewpoints, or one that moves. Astronomers measure the distance to some nearby stars by looking at them from two places half a year apart.

roots.thread: A single view is flat. Depth appears when two views are put side by side and the small differences between them are measured. Your two eyes do this all day, without telling you. Astronomers do it with two views half a year apart, to find how far away a star is. In both cases, distance is not something anyone looks at. It is something that is worked out from a difference.

teachings.source: Ibn al-Haytham, Book of Optics, Book 2
teachings.teaching: Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in Cairo about 1,000 years ago, wrote that we do not see distance and size directly. We judge them from clues, using memory and reasoning.
teachings.link: The brain works out depth from the difference between two views, and from clues such as size and overlap.

teachings.teaching: The Kena Upanishad asks what stands behind the senses. It speaks of the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, and the eye of the eye.
teachings.link: Eyes only catch light. The picture we see is built by something behind the eyes, and that something is the part of seeing nobody fully understands.

teachings.teaching: Plato, a Greek thinker about 2,400 years ago, told of people chained in a cave who see only shadows on a wall and think they are the whole world.
teachings.link: A single flat view can look like the whole world. A second view, or a view that moves, shows what is missing.

science.text: The brain works out depth from the small difference between the pictures of the two eyes, and from other clues such as size, overlap and movement of the head. This has been tested in many ways since Wheatstone in 1838.
How the brain turns these differences into the experience of a solid world around you is not known.

other_view.view: A robot car with two cameras measures distance by the same sums. There is nothing mysterious about it. Distance is really there in the world, and two cameras can measure it. To say that it is 'worked out' makes it sound less real than it is.

practice.title: Swap eyes and breathe
practice.say: Sit facing a wall. Hold up one finger at arm's length. Breathe in slowly. Close your left eye and look at the finger. Breathe out. Open your left eye and close the right. Notice the jump. Do this three times, slowly. Then open both eyes, and notice that you see one finger and one wall. Let yourself wonder who joined the two pictures.
practice.kid: Hold up a finger. Close one eye. Breathe in. Swap eyes. Breathe out. Do this three times. Then open both eyes. Who joined the two pictures?

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet done at home. Three Cards: the holes must be on one line and the room dim. The spot on the wall is small. Shifts of about 4 to 8 millimetres dim or stop the spot, and the numbers depend on your holes, so the table asks for what you really see. A grown-up makes the holes. Near Pencil, Far Pencil: you need a number strip on a wall and a helper to read the numbers. The jump at arm's length is about 15 centimetres for a child, and much more for a near pencil. If your child cannot hold the pencil still, rest the elbow on a table. The pencil-tip test usually gives 4 or 5 out of 5 with two eyes and fewer with one, but some children do well with one eye, which the step explains. Lens Makes a Window Picture: the picture is small and a little dim, so close the curtains on the other windows. The distance from lens to card for a window is about the focal length of the lens, 10 to 15 centimetres for a common magnifier. The change for a nearer thing is only a few centimetres. Never point the lens at the Sun. Hole in Your Hand works for most people in a few tries. The clock-face test needs a helper and a steady stare at the sticker. Near Point uses a card with small writing, not a pencil tip near the eye. The sign challenge needs a long corridor or a terrace. The Bird in a Cage works best with bold simple pictures drawn in the middle of each disc. Games and projects: Seeing Detectives has 24 cards and works with 2 to 4 players, with extra copies of the tokens. Facts to check before sharing: the octopus retina having no blind spot, the figure of about 1 person in 20 who cannot use two eyes together for depth, the near points by age, and the wording about time outdoors and short sight, which should follow a recent source.

quiz: Light travels in straight lines unless something bends it or bounces it.
That is why we cannot see round corners and why shadows have sharp edges.
Light bends round corners the way sound does.
Light waves are so tiny that they bend round edges by far too little to notice.
A lens bends the rays from each point of a thing back together to make a sharp picture.
When the rays meet again at one point, that point looks sharp, not blurry.
To look at a near thing, the lens inside the eye gets thinner.
The lens gets thicker to focus on near things and thinner for far things.
A far tree looks small because the rays from its top and bottom make a small angle.
The size a thing looks depends on that angle, and far things make smaller angles.
With short sight, the eye focuses in front of the retina, so far things look blurry.
Near things stay sharp, and glasses with a curved-in lens move the focus back.
Two eyes see slightly different pictures, and the brain uses the difference to judge distance.
Near things jump sideways more than far things when you switch eyes.
We have two eyes mainly so that we have a spare if one is hurt.
Two eyes also give depth from two views and a wider field of view.
Deer have both eyes at the front to judge distance for a pounce.
Deer are hunted animals, and eyes at the sides give them a wide view to spot danger.
The Moon really is bigger when it is near the horizon.
A photograph shows the same size in both places, so it is an illusion made by the brain.
odd: The first three show light going in straight lines, but sound bends round corners much more than light.
The first three are curved and bring rays together, but flat glass does not.
The first three hunt and have eyes in front for depth, but a deer is hunted and has eyes at the sides.
The first three need fine detail from the middle of the retina, but edge vision is poor at detail.
Focus falls in front of retina
The first three describe short sight, but curved-out glasses are the fix for long sight.
